body.text: sukhānvayo bodhisattvasya svaparārthaḥ katamaḥ / samāsataḥ pañcavidhena sukhena saṃgṛhīto veditavyaḥ / tatredaṃ pañcavidhaṃ sukham / hetusukhaṃ veditasukhaṃ duḥkhaprātipakṣikaṃ sukhaṃ veditopacchedasukhamavyabādhyañca pañcam sukham / tatra sukhapakṣyadvaya mindriyaṃ viṣayaśca / taddhetukaśca yaḥ sparśaḥ sukhavedanīyaḥ yacca kiñcidiṣṭaphalaṃ karma dṛṣṭe dharme abhisaṃparāye vā tatsarvamaikadhyamabhisaṃkṣipya hetusukhamityucyate / nāstyata uttari nāstyato bhūyaḥ / duḥkhapraśamanāpekṣaḥ ebhireva hetusukhasaṃgṛhītaistribhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ saṃbhūtaḥ kāyacittānugrahakaro 'nubhavo veditasukhamityucyate / tatpunaḥ samāsato dvividhaṃ sāsravamanāsravañca / tatra yadanāsravaṃ tacchaikṣamaśaikṣañca / sāsravaṃ punaḥ traidhātukaṃ kāmarūpārūpyapratisaṃyuktam / tatpunaḥ sarva traidhātukaṃ yathāyogaṃ ṣaḍvidhamāyatanabhedena cakṣuḥsaṃsparśajaṃ yāvanmanaḥsaṃsparśajam / tatpunaḥ ṣaḍvidhaṃ dvividham / kāyikaṃ caitasikañca / tatra pañcavijñānakāyasaṃprayuktaṃ kāyikaṃ manovijñānasaṃprayuktaṃ caitasikam / śītoṣṇakṣutpipāsādikānāmanekavidhānāṃ duḥkhānāṃ bahunānāprakārāṇāmutpannotpannānāṃ
body.translated_text: What is the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s own and others' benefit that is conducive to happiness (<s>sukhānvaya</s>)? In brief, it should be understood as comprised of fivefold happiness. There, this is the fivefold happiness: causal happiness (<s>hetusukha</s>), experienced happiness (<s>veditasukha</s>), happiness that counteracts suffering (<s>duḥkhaprātipakṣika sukha</s>), happiness of the cessation of experience (<s>veditopaccheda sukha</s>), and inviolable happiness (<s>avyābādhya sukha</s>) as the fifth. There, the pair of factors on the side of happiness are the faculty (<s>indriya</s>) and the sense-object (<s>viṣaya</s>); and their cause—the contact (<s>sparśa</s>) that is to be felt as pleasant, and whatever wholesome <s>karma</s> producing a desired result either in this life or in future lives—all of that, gathered together, is called causal happiness. There is nothing higher, nothing beyond this. The experience—produced by these very three causes comprised in causal happiness, in dependence on the pacification of suffering, and conducive to the ease of body and mind—is called experienced happiness. That, again, is in brief twofold: with outflows (<s>sāsrava</s>) and without outflows (<s>anāsrava</s>). There, that which is without outflows is both that of one in training (<s>śaikṣa</s>) and that of one beyond training (<s>aśaikṣa</s>). That with outflows, moreover, belongs to the three realms—connected with the desire-realm, form-realm, and formless-realm (<s>Kāma</s>-, <s>Rūpa</s>-, <s>Ārūpya</s>-). That, moreover, belonging entirely to the three realms, is sixfold according to the division of sense-bases: born of eye-contact, up to born of mind-contact. That sixfold [happiness] is again twofold: bodily and mental. There, that associated with the five consciousness-groups is bodily; that associated with mental consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>) is mental. Of the many and various kinds of suffering—cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the like—as they arise again and again,

body.text: śītoṣṇakṣutpipāsādiduḥkhapratikāreṇa praśamāt tasminneva duḥkhopaśamamātrake yā sukhabuddhirutpadyate idamucyate duḥkhaprātipakṣikaṃ sukham / saṃjñāveditanirodhasamāpattirveditopacchedasukhamityucyate / avyābādhyasukhaṃ punaḥ samāsataścaturākāraṃ veditavyam / naiṣkramyasukhaṃpravivekasukhamupaśamasukhaṃ saṃbodhisukhañca / samyageva śraddhayā agārādanāgārikāṃ pravrajitasya āgārikavicitravyāsaṅgaduḥkhanirmokṣānnaiṣkramyasukhamityucyate / kāmapāpakākuśaladharmaprahāṇavivekātprathame dhyāne vivekajaṃ prītisukhaṃ pravivekasukhamityucyate / dvitīyādiṣu dhyāneṣu vitarkavicāropaśamādu paśamasukhamityucyate / sarvakleśātyantavisaṃyogājjñeyavastuyathābhūtābhisaṃbodhācca yatsukhamidamucyate saṃbodhisukham /
body.translated_text: Through the counteraction of sufferings such as cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so forth, from the pacification [of those], that cognition of pleasure which arises in mere cessation of suffering—this is called pleasure that is the antidote to suffering (<s>duḥkhaprātipakṣikam sukham</s>). The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (<s>saṃjñāveditanirodhasamāpatti</s>) is called the pleasure of the cessation of feeling (<s>veditopacchedasukham</s>). The pleasure of freedom from affliction (<s>avyābādhyasukham</s>), moreover, should be understood in brief as fourfold: the pleasure of renunciation (<s>naiṣkramyasukham</s>), the pleasure of seclusion (<s>pravivekasukham</s>), the pleasure of pacification (<s>upaśamasukham</s>), and the pleasure of awakening (<s>saṃbodhisukham</s>). For one who has rightly gone forth from the household to the homeless life through faith, the pleasure arising from liberation from the varied entanglements and sufferings of household life is called the pleasure of renunciation. In the first <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), from the seclusion through abandonment of evil, unwholesome <s>dharmas</s> of sensual desire, the joy and pleasure born of seclusion is called the pleasure of seclusion. In the second and subsequent <s>dhyānas</s>, from the pacification of discursive and sustained thought, it is called the pleasure of pacification. From the ultimate and complete separation from all afflictions, and from the awakening to the true nature of knowable objects—the pleasure that arises from this is called the pleasure of awakening.

body.text: tatra hetusukhaṃ sukhahetutvāt sukhaṃ na svabhāvataḥ / veditasukhaṃ na hetubhāvādapi tu svabhāvata eva / duḥkha-prātipakṣikaṃ sukhaṃ na ca hetubhāvānnāpi svabhāvataḥ api tu duḥkhopaśama-mātrad duḥkhāpakarṣaṇāt sukham / veditopacchedasukhaṃ na hetubhāvānna svābhāvyānna duḥkhāpakarṣaṇādapi tu yatkiṃcidveditam / idamatra duḥkhasyeti kṛtvā pāramārthikasya duḥkhasya tāvatkālikvavihāra-vyupaśamāt sukham / avyābādhya-sukha-saṃgṛhītaṃ paścimaṃ saṃbodhisukhamāyatyāṃ ca tasyaiva pāramārthikasya duḥkhasyātyanta-vyupaśamād dṛṣṭe ca dharme sarva-kleśa-pakṣyasya dauṣṭhulyagyāśrayagatasyātyantoparamāt sukham / tadavaśiṣṭamavyābādhya-sukhaṃ tasyaiva paścimasyānukūlatvāt tatpakṣyatvāt tadāvāhakatvāt avyābādhyasukhaṃ veditavyam /
body.translated_text: There, the pleasure of cause is pleasure because it is the cause of pleasure, not by its own nature. The pleasure of feeling is [pleasure] not from being a cause, but by its own nature indeed. The pleasure that is the antidote to suffering is [pleasure] neither from being a cause nor by its own nature, but is pleasure merely from the cessation of suffering, from the removal of suffering. The pleasure of the cessation of feeling is [pleasure] neither from being a cause, nor from its own nature, nor from the removal of suffering, but rather because whatever is felt—'this here is suffering'—through the temporary cessation of abiding in that ultimate suffering, it is pleasure. The last pleasure of awakening, included in the pleasure of freedom from affliction, is pleasure both in the future, from the ultimate and complete cessation of that very ultimate suffering, and in the present life, from the ultimate subsiding of the entire basis of the state of impairment (<s>dauṣṭhulya</s>) belonging to the side of all afflictions. The remaining pleasure of freedom from affliction should be understood as the pleasure of freedom from affliction because of its conformity to that last [pleasure], because of belonging to its class, and because of leading to it.

body.text: tatra bodhisattvo yadeva hitapakṣyaṃ sukhaṃ tadeva sattvānāmupasaṃharet natu ahitapakṣyam / ahitapakṣyaṃ punaḥ sukhaṃ yathābhūtaṃ samyakprajñayā parijñāya tasmāt sattvān vicchandayecchaktitaśca tasyāpakarṣāpahārāya vyāyaccheta / duḥkhānugatamapi yaddhitaṃ syāt tadvodhisattvena sahaiva duḥkhena sahaiva daurmanasyenākāmakānāṃ sattvānāmupasaṃhartavyamupāyakauśalya-saṃniśrayeṇa / sukhānugatañcāpi yadahitaṃ syāttadapi sahaiva sukhena saha saumanasyena kāmakānāṃ sattvānāmapahartavyamapakarṣitavya mupāyakauśalya-saṃniśrayeṇa / tatkasya hetauḥ / sukhāyaiva sa
body.translated_text: There, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> should bring to beings only that pleasure which belongs to the side of benefit, and not that which belongs to the side of non-benefit. Having discerned the pleasure belonging to the side of non-benefit as it truly is, with correct wisdom, one should dissuade beings from it and exert oneself according to one's ability for its removal and elimination. Even what is accompanied by suffering, if it would be beneficial, should be brought by the <s>Bodhisattva</s> to unwilling beings together with the suffering and together with the displeasure, relying on skill in means (<s>upāyakauśalya</s>). And even what is accompanied by pleasure, if it would be non-beneficial, should also be taken away and removed from willing beings together with the pleasure and together with the gratification, relying on skill in means. For what reason? Because that is to be understood as definitely leading to

body.text: āyatyāṃ sattvānāṃ niyato veditavyaḥ / yo 'sau duḥkhena saha hitopasaṃhāraḥ sukhena ca sahāhitāpakarṣaḥ / ataeva bodhisattvaḥ sattveṣu yo hitakāmaḥ arthataḥ sukhakāmo 'pi sa jñeyaḥ / yo hitapradaḥ sukhaprado 'pi sa jñeyaḥ / tathā hi hitaṃ hetusthānīyaṃ sukhaṃ phalasthānīyam / tasmātsukhānugata eva sa sattveṣu veditavyaḥ / yaḥ kaściddhitānugataḥ tatra yacceṣṭaphalaṃ karma dṛṣṭe dharme abhisaṃparāye ca hetusukhasaṃgṛhītaṃ yacca duḥkhaprātipakṣikaṃ yacca vedito pacchedasukhaṃ yaccāvyābādhyasukham etadekāntena nirvimarṣo bodhisattvaḥ sattveṣūpasaṃharet / etaddhyanugrāhakaṃ cānavadyañca / vedita sukhamindriyaviṣayasparśasaṃgṛhītañca hetusukhaṃ yatsaṃkleśāya vā kliṣṭaṃ vā sāvadyamahitamapathyaṃ tannopasaṃharet / yatpunarasaṃkleśāyāsaṃkliṣṭaṃ vā 'navadyaṃ hitaṃ pathyaṃ ca tadvodhisattvaḥ sattveṣūpasaṃhared yathāśakti yathābalam / api cātmanā tathaiva samācarecchikṣeta pratyanubhavedityayaṃ bodhisattvānāṃ hitasukhānvayaḥ svaparārtho veditavyaḥ / nāta uttari nāto bhūyaḥ /
body.translated_text: the pleasure of beings in the future—namely, the bringing of benefit together with suffering and the removal of non-benefit together with pleasure. Therefore, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> who desires the benefit of beings is, in truth, to be known as one who desires their pleasure also; one who gives benefit is to be known as one who gives pleasure also. For benefit stands in the position of cause, and pleasure stands in the position of result. Therefore, one should understand that [the <s>Bodhisattva</s>] is indeed oriented toward the pleasure of beings—whoever is oriented toward their benefit. Therein, whatever is the intended result of action, in this life and the hereafter, included in the pleasure of cause, and whatever is the pleasure that is the antidote to suffering, and whatever is the pleasure of the cessation of feeling, and whatever is the pleasure of freedom from affliction—all this the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, without reservation, should bring to beings. For this is beneficial and blameless. But the pleasure of feeling—that which is included in sense-faculty contact with objects, and the pleasure of cause—that which leads to defilement or is defiled, blameworthy, non-beneficial, and unwholesome, that one should not bring. But what does not lead to defilement, is undefiled, blameless, beneficial, and wholesome—that the <s>Bodhisattva</s> should bring to beings according to one's ability and strength. Moreover, one should oneself practice in the same way, train, and experience [it accordingly]—this should be understood as the connection of the <s>Bodhisattvas</s>' [practice with] benefit and pleasure, for oneself and others. There is nothing beyond this, nothing more.

body.text: tatra katamo bodhisattvasya hetuphalasaṃgṛhītaḥ svaparārthaḥ / samāsatastrividho hetustrividhameva ca phalaṃ veditavyam / vipākahetuḥ vipākaphalaṃ puṇyahetuḥ puṇyaphalaṃ jñānahetuḥ jñānaphalam /
body.translated_text: There, what is the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s benefit for self and others, included in cause and result? In brief, the cause is threefold and the result likewise is to be understood as threefold: the cause of ripening (<s>vipākahetu</s>) and the result of ripening (<s>vipākaphala</s>); the cause of merit (<s>puṇyahetu</s>) and the result of merit (<s>puṇyaphala</s>); the cause of knowledge (<s>jñānahetu</s>) and the result of knowledge (<s>jñānaphala</s>).

body.text: vipākaḥ katamaḥ / samāsato 'ṣṭavidho vipākaḥ / āyuḥsaṃpat varṇasaṃpat kulasaṃpat aiśvaryasaṃpat ādeyavākyatā maheśākhyatā manuṣyatvaṃ balameva cāṣṭamam / dīrghāyuṣkaṃ cirasthitikatā bodhisattvasyāyuḥsaṃpat / abhirūpatā darśanīyatā prāsādikatvaṃ varṇasaṃpat / ucceṣu kuleṣu pratyājātiḥ kulasaṃpat / mahābhogatā mahāpakṣatā mahāparivāritā ca aiśvaryasaṃpat / yatpunaḥ śraddheyo bhavati pratyayitaḥ sattvānāmutpannotpanneṣvadhikaraṇeṣu prāmāṇikatvena ratheyaḥ kāṃsakūṭatūlākūṭādibhinirmāyāśāṭhyena / nikṣipyasya ca draviṇasyānabhidroho bhavatyavisaṃvādakaḥ / tannidānañca sattvānāṃ gṛhītavākyo bhavati / iyamucyate ādeyavacanatā / mahadyaśaḥ khyātiścāsya loke prathitā bhavati yaduta śauryaṃ vā vīrya vā dhairyaṃ vā vaicakṣaṇyaṃ vā naipuṇyaṃ vā sauśīlyaṃ vā vicitraśilpakarmasthānātirekataratama-kauśalyaṃ vā ārabhya /
body.translated_text: What is the ripening (<s>vipāka</s>)? In brief, the ripening is eightfold: excellence of lifespan (<s>āyuḥsaṃpat</s>), excellence of complexion (<s>varṇasaṃpat</s>), excellence of family (<s>kulasaṃpat</s>), excellence of sovereignty (<s>aiśvaryasaṃpat</s>), being one whose words are heeded (<s>ādeyavākyatā</s>), great renown (<s>maheśākhyatā</s>), human birth (<s>manuṣyatvam</s>), and strength (<s>bala</s>) as the eighth. The <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s excellence of lifespan is long life and enduring existence. Excellence of complexion is being handsome, good-looking, and inspiring confidence. Excellence of family is being born in high families. Excellence of sovereignty is having great wealth, a great following, and a great retinue. As for being one whose words are heeded: that one becomes trustworthy, relied upon by beings in matters that arise as authoritative—regarded as a standard, like [one tested by] touchstone, scale, and the like—without fabrication or deceit; and one does not betray the wealth placed in one's keeping and is not deceptive; and because of that, beings accept one's words—this is called having one's words heeded (<s>ādeyavacanatā</s>). Great fame and renown are spread abroad in the world, with respect to valor, vigor, courage, discernment, skill, good character, and supreme expertise in various arts and crafts.

body.text: tannidānañca gururbhavati mahājanakāyasya satkaraṇīyo gurukaraṇīyo mānanīyaḥ pūjanīyaḥ / iyamucyate maheśākhyatā / puruṣabhāvaḥ puruṣendriyeṇa samanvāgato manuṣyatvam / alpābādhatā arogajātīyatā mahotsāhatā ca prakṛtyā balasaṃpat /
body.translated_text: Because of that, one becomes weighty for a great multitude of people—worthy of respect, veneration, honor, and worship. This is called great renown (<s>maheśākhyatā</s>). Manhood (<s>manuṣyatvam</s>) is the state of being a man, endowed with the male faculty. Excellence of strength is being by nature free from illness, of a healthy constitution, and of great energy.

body.text: vipākahetuḥ katamaḥ ahiṃsā sattveṣvahiṃsāśayaścāyuḥsaṃpado hetuḥ / ālokaśucivastradānaṃ varṇasaṃpado hetuḥ / nihatamānatā sattveṣu kuśalasaṃpado hetuḥ / dānamarthiṣu copakaraṇavikaleṣu caiśvaryasaṃpado hetuḥ / satyavacano 'piśunā 'paruṣā 'saṃbhinnapralāpābhyāsaḥ ādeyavacanatāyā hetuḥ / āyatyāmātmani vicitraguṇādhānapraṇidhānavato ratnatrayapūjā gurupūjā maheśākhyatāyā hetuḥ / manuṣyabhāve cābhiratiḥ strībhāve vidveṣaśca / tatrādīnavadarśinaḥ / pareṣāñca manuṣyatvopasaṃhārau dvābhyāṃ kāraṇābhyām / vicchandanatayā ca strīṇāṃ strībhāvābhiratānāṃ [ca] strībhāvāt / vinirmokṣaṇatayā ca dharmeṇa puruṣendriyavipralopāyopāttānāmupanītānāṃ manuṣyāṇāṃ manuṣyatvasya hetuḥ / kāyena sattvānāṃ vaiyāvṛtya kriyā sahāyakriyā utpannotpanneṣu kṛtyeṣu yathāśakti yathābalaṃ dharmeṇāsāhasena bhakta-tarpaṇa-yavāgupānānāṃ ca vṛṣyāṇāmutsāhakarāṇāmannapānānāṃ sattveṣūpasaṃhāro balasampado hetuḥ / ityaṣṭavidhasya vipākasyāyamaṣṭavidho heturveditavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: What is the cause of ripening? Non-harming of beings and the intention of non-harming is the cause of excellence of lifespan. Giving of light, clean garments is the cause of excellence of complexion. Humility toward beings is the cause of excellence of good family. Giving to supplicants and to those lacking provisions is the cause of excellence of sovereignty. The practice of truthful speech, non-slandering, non-harshness, and non-frivolous talk is the cause of having one's words heeded. Worship of the Three Jewels, worship of teachers, and the aspiration and vow to establish various qualities in oneself in the future are the cause of great renown. Delight in the male state and aversion to the female state, seeing the disadvantages therein; and bringing others to human birth for two reasons—by dissuading women who delight in womanhood from the female state, and by liberating through the <s>Dharma</s> those human beings whose male faculty has been seized or led away from them—this is the cause of human birth. Physical service to beings, assisting them, and in their arising needs, according to one's ability and strength, through righteous means and without violence, providing nourishing foods, gruels, drinks, and energizing and invigorating food and drink to beings—this is the cause of excellence of strength. Thus, this eightfold cause of the eightfold ripening should be understood.

body.text: sa punarayaṃ hetuḥ samāsatastribhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ puṣṭo bhavati paripūrṇasya puṣṭasyodārasya vipākasyābhinirvṛttaye / trīṇi kāraṇāni katamāni / cittaśuddhiḥ prayoga śuddhiḥ kṣetraśuddhiśca / tatra yā ca śuddhāśayatā anuttarāyāṃ samyaksaṃbodhau teṣāṃ kuśalamūlānāṃ pariṇamanād yā ca tīvrāśayatā ghanarasenodāreṇa prasādenādhyācaraṇād yā ca sahadhārmikasya darśanenābhipramodanā yā ca pratidivasaṃ pratikṣaṇaṃ tadanudharmameva bahulamanuvitarkaṇānuvicāraṇā / iyamucyate cittaśuddhiḥ / tatra yo dīrghakālābhyāso nirantarakāritā [ca] nipuṇakāritā ca pareṣāñcāsamātte tasmin kuśale samādāpanāya varṇavāditā samātte vā punaḥ saṃharṣaṇāya varṇavāditā teṣāmeva ca tasmin kuśalamūle sanniveśanā pratiṣṭhāpanā /
body.translated_text: That cause, moreover, is nourished in brief by three conditions for the production of a complete, nourished, and magnificent ripening. What are the three conditions? Purity of mind (<s>cittaśuddhi</s>), purity of application (<s>prayogaśuddhi</s>), and purity of field (<s>kṣetraśuddhi</s>). There, the purity of intention toward the unsurpassed, perfect awakening—through the dedication of those roots of virtue, the intensity of intention with dense, rich, and magnificent faith in the practice, the delight through seeing a fellow practitioner of the <s>Dharma</s>, and the daily and momentary frequent reflection and deliberation in accordance with that very <s>Dharma</s>—this is called purity of mind. There, the long-term practice, the uninterrupted performance, the refined performance, and the praising of others to encourage them in the undertaking of that wholesome [practice] when they have not yet undertaken it, or the praising to inspire those who have already undertaken it, and the establishing and grounding of those [beings] in those very roots of virtue—

body.text: iyamucyate prayogaśuddhiḥ / tatra samāsataḥ prayogasya samyaksampādanāttasyaiva ca samyakprayogasya phale 'vasthāpanā tkṣetraśuddhirveditavyā /
body.translated_text: this is called purity of application. There, in brief, purity of field should be understood as the correct accomplishment of application and the establishing of that very correct application in its result.

body.text: tatra vipākaphalaṃ katamat / āyuḥsaṃpanno bodhisattvo dīrghakālaṃ kuśalapakṣe prayujyate prabhūtañca kuśalamūlopacayaṃ karoti svārtha parārthañcārabhya / idamāyuḥsaṃpadaḥ phalam / varṇasaṃpanno bodhisattvaḥ priyo bhavati mahājanakāyasya / priyatvāccābhigamanīyo bhavati / tayā ca manojñarūpatayā sammukhībhāvopagamanāccāsya mahājanakāyo vacanaṃ śrotavyaṃ kartavyaṃ manyate / idaṃ varṇasaṃpadaḥ phalaṃ bodhisattvasya veditavyam / kulasaṃpanno bodhisattvaḥ sammato bhavati mahājanakāyasya pūjyaśca praśasyaśca / sammatatvācca pūjyatvātpraśasyatvād yatra yatra vastuni sattvān samādāpayati te tejograstāstatra tatrāśu pratipadyante na vivadante na viceṣṭante 'kriyāyai / idaṃ kulasaṃpadaḥ phalaṃ bodhisattvasya veditavyam / aiśvaryasaṃpanno bodhisattvo dānena sattvān saṃgṛhṇāti paripācayati / idamaiśvaryasaṃpado bodhisattvasya phalaṃ veditavyam / ādeyavacano bodhisattvaḥ priyavāditayā arthacaryayā samānārthatayā ca sattvān gṛhṇāti paripācayati / idamādeyavacanatāyā bodhisattvasya phalaṃ veditavyam / maheśākhyo bodhisattvaḥ sattvānāṃ vicitraiḥ kṛtyakaraṇīyaiḥ sahāyībhāvaṃ gacchannupakārī bhavati / yenopakāre ṇāvabaddhacittāḥ sattvā asya gauravāt kṛtajñatayā ca laghuladhvevājñāmanuvartante satkṛtyādareṇa / idaṃ maheśākhyatāyā bodhisattvasya phalaṃ veditavyam / manuṣyabhūto bodhisattvaḥ purūṣendriyeṇa samanvāgato bhājanabhūto bhavati sarvaguṇānāṃ sarvavyavasāyānāṃ sarvajñeyapravicayānām / viśāradaśca bhavatyanāvṛtagatiḥ sarvasattvasarvakālopasaṃkramaṇasaṃbhāṣaṇasaṃvāsasaṃbhogaraho vihārāṇam idaṃ puruṣatva phalaṃ bodhisattvasya veditavyam / balasaṃpanno bodhisattvaḥ akhinno bhavati kuśaladharmārjanaprayogeṇa sattvānugrahaprayogeṇa ca / ārabdhavīryaśca bhavati dṛḍhavīryaḥ kṣiprābhijñaśca bhavati / idaṃ balasaṃpado bodhisattvasya phalaṃ veditavyam / itīdaṃ bodhisattvānāmaṣṭavidhasya vipākasyāṣṭavidhaṃ phalaṃ yadbhavati sattvānāṃ
body.translated_text: There, what is the result of ripening? The <s>Bodhisattva</s> endowed with excellence of lifespan engages in the wholesome side for a long time and accumulates abundant roots of virtue, with reference to benefit for self and others. This is the result of excellence of lifespan. The <s>Bodhisattva</s> endowed with excellence of complexion becomes dear to a great multitude of people; and because of being dear, one is approachable; and because of that pleasing appearance and the approach of coming face to face, the great multitude of people considers one's words worthy of hearing and acting upon. This should be understood as the result of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s excellence of complexion. The <s>Bodhisattva</s> endowed with excellence of family becomes respected by a great multitude of people, and is honored and praised; and because of being respected, honored, and praised, wherever and in whatever matter one instructs beings, they, overcome by [one's] authority, quickly comply and do not dispute or resist through inaction. This should be understood as the result of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s excellence of family. The <s>Bodhisattva</s> endowed with excellence of sovereignty gathers and matures beings through generosity. This should be understood as the result of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s excellence of sovereignty. The <s>Bodhisattva</s> whose words are heeded gathers and matures beings through pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and practice of equal purpose. This should be understood as the result of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s having one's words heeded. The <s>Bodhisattva</s> of great renown, by assisting beings in their various tasks and duties, becomes a benefactor; through that benefaction, beings whose minds are bound [to one] out of respect and gratitude very easily follow one's instructions with reverence and care. This should be understood as the result of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s great renown. The <s>Bodhisattva</s> who is a human being, endowed with the male faculty, becomes a vessel for all qualities, all undertakings, and all investigations of the knowable; and one becomes confident, with unobstructed movement, worthy of approaching, conversing with, dwelling with, and enjoying [the company of] all beings at all times. This should be understood as the result of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s manhood. The <s>Bodhisattva</s> endowed with excellence of strength is unwearied in the endeavor of acquiring wholesome <s>dharmas</s> and in the endeavor of benefiting beings; and one becomes energetically vigorous, firmly vigorous, and quick in attaining higher knowledges (<s>abhijñā</s>). This should be understood as the result of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s excellence of strength. Thus, this is the eightfold result of the eightfold ripening of the <s>Bodhisattvas</s>, which exists for beings

body.text: copakārāya buddhadharmāṇāścodayāyānukūlamanuguṇam / asmin khalu bodhisattvo vipākaphale vyavasthitaḥ svayañca śakto bhavati pratibalaḥ sattvānāṃ vicitraprabhūtārthakaraṇe / te 'pi cāsya vineyā niyojyā bhavanti yathākāmakaraṇīyāya yaduta svārthakriyāmārabhya / svayañcedayaṃ bodhisattvaḥ pratibalaḥ syādvineyāścāsya na niyojyā bhaveyuḥ / evamasya na pracurā syānna pradakṣiṇā parārthakriyā yenāyaṃ na śaknuyāt parārthaṃ kartum / svayañcedayaṃ bodhisattvaḥ aśaktaḥ syādapratibalo vineyāścāsya niyojyāḥ syuḥ svārthakriyāmārabhyaivamapi bodhisattvasya parārthakriyā na pracurā na pradakṣiṇā syād yenāyaṃ na śaknuyāt parārtha kartum / tasmādubhayasānnidhye ubhayasaṃpadiṃ satyāṃ bodhisattvasya sattvārthakriyā pracurā bhavati pradakṣiṇā yena śaknoti parārthaṃ kartum / tathābhūtaścāsau bodhisattvaḥ ātmanaśca buddhadharmān sattvāṃśca triṣu yāneṣu kṣiprameva paripācayati / ātmanā cānuttarāṃ samyaksaṃbodhimadhisaṃbudhyate / paripakvāṃśca sattvān vimocayati / tadanena paryāyeṇa bodhisattvānāṃ yasmādaṣṭavidhaṃ vipākaphalaṃ hitasukhāya sattvānāṃ saṃvartate / tasmād yaḥ sarvasattvānāṃ bandhyo nirarthaḥ saṃsāraḥ sa teṣāmavandhyaśca mahārthaśca bhavati /
body.translated_text: and for the benefit and encouragement of <s>Buddha</s>-qualities, in a favorable and concordant manner. Indeed, a <s>Bodhisattva</s> established in this ripened fruit (<s>vipākaphala</s>) is personally capable and powerful in accomplishing various and abundant purposes for beings. And those to be trained by him become amenable to being directed as he wishes, namely beginning with their own welfare. If this <s>Bodhisattva</s> were personally capable and powerful, but those to be trained by him were not amenable, then his activity for the benefit of others would not be abundant or successful, and he would be unable to accomplish the benefit of others. And if this <s>Bodhisattva</s> were personally incapable and powerless, but those to be trained by him were amenable to being directed for their own welfare—even so, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s activity for the benefit of others would not be abundant or successful, and he would be unable to accomplish the benefit of others. Therefore, when both are present, when both endowments are met, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s activity for the welfare of beings becomes abundant and successful, and he is able to accomplish the benefit of others. And such a <s>Bodhisattva</s> swiftly brings to maturity both <s>Buddha</s>-qualities for himself and beings in the three vehicles. He himself fully awakens to the unsurpassed, perfect awakening (<s>anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi</s>), and liberates beings who have been brought to maturity. Therefore, by this method, since the eightfold ripened fruit of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> conduces to the welfare and happiness of beings, that <s>saṃsāra</s> which is barren and purposeless for all beings becomes for them fruitful and greatly purposeful.

body.text: tatra katamat puṇyam / katamajjñānam / puṇyamucyate samāsatastisraḥ pāramitāḥ / dānapāramitā śīlapāramitā kṣāntipāramitā ca / jñānaṃ punarekā pāramitā yaduta prajñāpāramitā / vīryapāramitā dhyānapāramitā ca puṇyapakṣyā jñānapakṣyā ca veditavyā / yadvīrya niśritya dānaṃ dadāti śīlaṃ vā samādatte rakṣati maitryādīni cāpramāṇāni bhāvayati / idamevaṃbhāgīyaṃ puṇyapakṣyaṃ vīryam / yatpunarvīryaṃ niśritya śrutacintābhāvanāmayyāṃ prajñāyāṃ yogaṃ karoti skandhakauśalyaṃ vā karoti dhātukauśalyamāyatanakauśalyaṃ pratītyasamutpādakuśalyaṃ sthānāsthānakauśalyaṃ duḥkhaṃ vā duḥkhataḥ samudayaṃ vā samudayato nirodhaṃ vā nirodhato mārgaṃ vā mārgataḥ pratyavekṣate / kuśalākuśalāndharmān sāvadyānanavadyān hīnapraṇītān kṛṣṇaśuklasapravibhāgapratītyasamutpannān dharmān yathābhūtaṃ pravicinoti pratyavekṣate / idamucyate jñānapakṣyaṃ vīryam / yaddhyānaṃ niśrityaṃ dānaṃ vā dadāti śīlaṃ vā samādatte rakṣati maitryādīni cāpramāṇāni bhāvayati / idamevaṃbhāgīyaṃ puṇyapakṣyaṃ dhyānam /
body.translated_text: There, what is merit (<s>puṇya</s>)? What is knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>)? Merit, in brief, is said to be three <s>pāramitās</s>: the perfection of generosity (<s>dānapāramitā</s>), the perfection of moral conduct (<s>śīlapāramitā</s>), and the perfection of patience (<s>kṣāntipāramitā</s>). Knowledge, on the other hand, is one <s>pāramitā</s>, namely the perfection of wisdom (<s>prajñāpāramitā</s>). The perfection of vigor (<s>vīryapāramitā</s>) and the perfection of meditation (<s>dhyānapāramitā</s>) should be understood as belonging to both the side of merit and the side of knowledge. The vigor by relying on which one gives gifts, takes up and guards moral conduct, and cultivates the immeasurables (<s>apramāṇa</s>) such as loving-kindness (<s>maitrī</s>) and so forth—this is vigor belonging to the side of merit. The vigor, however, by relying on which one engages in the practice of wisdom born of learning, reflection, and cultivation (<s>śrutacintābhāvanāmayī prajñā</s>), or develops skill in the aggregates (<s>skandhakauśalya</s>), skill in the elements (<s>dhātukauśalya</s>), skill in the sense-bases (<s>āyatanakauśalya</s>), skill in dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpādakauśalya</s>), skill in the possible and impossible (<s>sthānāsthānakauśalya</s>), or examines and investigates suffering as suffering, the origin as origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as path; or discriminates and investigates as they truly are <s>dharmas</s> that are wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, inferior and superior, dark and bright, with their divisions, and dependently arisen—this is called vigor belonging to the side of knowledge. The meditation by relying on which one gives gifts, takes up and guards moral conduct, and cultivates the immeasurables such as loving-kindness and so forth—this is meditation belonging to the side of merit.

body.text: yatpunardhyānaṃ niśritya śrutacintābhāvanāyyāṃ prajñāyāṃ yogaṃ karoti skandhakauśalyaṃ vā pūrvavat sarvaṃ vaktavyaṃ tadyathā vīrye / idamucyate jñānapakṣyaṃ dhyānam / taccaitat puṇyajñānaṃ samāsataḥ ṣaḍvidhaṃ bhavati / apramāṇaṃ tvetadekaikaprabhedato veditavyam /
body.translated_text: The meditation, however, by relying on which one engages in the practice of wisdom born of learning, reflection, and cultivation, or develops skill in the aggregates—everything should be stated as before, as in the case of vigor—this is called meditation belonging to the side of knowledge. That merit and knowledge, in brief, is sixfold. But it should be understood as immeasurable with regard to the divisions of each individual [category].

body.text: puṇyajñānahetuḥ katamaḥ / samāsatastrayaḥ puṇyajñānahetavo veditavyāḥ / puṇyajñānapratilambhasthānopacayāya yacchandaḥ anukūlo 'vidhuraḥ pratyayaḥ pūrvakaśca puṇyajñānābhyāsaḥ / tatrāyamavidhuraḥ pratyayaḥ yā viparītasya ca pratyayasyāpratyupasthānamasannihitatā / aviparītasya ca pratyayasya pratyupasthānaṃ sannihitatā / tatra yā pāpamitramāgamya viparītā puṇyajñānadeśanā viparītena vā manaskāreṇa viparītagrāhitā / idamucyate viparītapratyasānnidhyam / etadviparyayeṇa śuklapakṣeṇa aviparītapratyayasānnidhyaṃ veditavyam / ye ca puṇyajñānapratilambhasthityupacayāya prayuktasyāntarāyāḥ / teṣāñca vivarjanamanutpādaḥ pratyayo 'vidhura ityucyate bodhisattvasya puṇyajñānayoḥ / eṣāṃ trayāṇāṃ hetūnāmanyatamavaikalyānnāpi puṇyasya nāpi jñānasya prasūtirveditavyā /
body.translated_text: What is the cause of merit and knowledge (<s>puṇyajñānahetu</s>)? In brief, three causes of merit and knowledge should be understood: the desire (<s>chanda</s>) for the attainment, abiding, and increase of merit and knowledge; the favorable, unimpaired condition (<s>avidhura pratyaya</s>); and the prior practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) of merit and knowledge. There, this is the unimpaired condition: the non-arising and absence of adverse conditions, and the arising and presence of non-adverse conditions. There, the perverted teaching of merit and knowledge through contact with an evil friend (<s>pāpamitra</s>), or that which is grasped in a perverted way through perverted attention—this is called the presence of a perverted condition. Its opposite, on the side of the wholesome, should be understood as the presence of a non-perverted condition. And the avoidance and non-arising of those obstacles for one engaged in the attainment, abiding, and increase of merit and knowledge—this is called the unimpaired condition for the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s merit and knowledge. When any one of these three causes is deficient, neither the arising of merit nor of knowledge should be understood [as occurring].

body.text: puṇyajñānaphalaṃ katamat / puṇyamāśritya bodhisattvo 'kṣataḥ saṃsāre saṃsarati nātyarthaṃ duḥkhairbādhyamānaḥ / yathepsitañca sattvārthaṃ sattvānugrahaṃ śaknoti kartum / jñānamāśritya bodhisattvaḥ samyak puṇyaparigrahaṃ karoti na mithyā vicitrāprameyakauśalyakriyayā ca yāvadanuttarāṃ samyaksaṃbodhimabhisaṃbudhyate / itīdaṃ samāsena puṇyajñānaphalaṃ yathāyogaṃ caturvidhaṃ veditavyam / apramāṇantve tatprakāraprabhedataḥ /
body.translated_text: What is the fruit of merit and knowledge (<s>puṇyajñānaphala</s>)? Relying on merit, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> wanders in <s>saṃsāra</s> unharmed, not excessively oppressed by sufferings. And one is able to accomplish the desired welfare and assistance of beings. Relying on knowledge, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> correctly takes up the collection of merit, not wrongly, and through the activity of various and immeasurable skills, one fully awakens to the unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Thus, in brief, the fruit of merit and knowledge should be understood as fourfold, according to the context. But it is immeasurable with regard to the divisions of each type.

body.text: tatra yaśca vipāko yaśca vipākaheturyacca vipākaphalaṃ sarvametatpuṇyāśritaṃ puṇyaprabhavam / puṇyaṃ punarjñānāśritaṃ jñānaprabhavam tasmādubhayametatpradhānamanuttarāyai samyaksaṃbodhaye / puṇyaṃ pradhānaṃ jñānaṃ punarnirūttaram puṇyajñānaṃ tadanyataravaikalyādayaṃ bodhisattvo 'nuttarāṃ samyaksaṃbodhiṃ nādhigacchet / ityayaṃ bodhisattvasya hetuphalasaṃgṛhītaḥ svaparārtho veditavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: There, the ripening (<s>vipāka</s>), the cause of ripening (<s>vipākahetu</s>), and the fruit of ripening (<s>vipākaphala</s>)—all this is dependent on merit and arises from merit. Merit, in turn, is dependent on knowledge and arises from knowledge. Therefore, both are principal for the unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Merit is principal; knowledge, however, is supreme. Without either merit or knowledge, this <s>Bodhisattva</s> would not attain the unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Thus, this self-and-other benefit of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, encompassed by cause and fruit, should be understood.

body.text: tatra katamo bodhisattvasya dṛṣṭadhārmikaḥ svaparārthaḥ / katamaḥ sāṃparāyikaḥ / yuktena śilpasthānakarmasthānena puruṣakāreṇa yā bhogānāmarjanā / teṣāmeva copārjitānāṃ bhogānāṃ mātrayopabhogaḥ / pūrvakasya ceṣṭaphalasya karmaṇo vipakvavipākasya
body.translated_text: There, what is the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s benefit for self and others in the present life (<s>dṛṣṭadhārmika</s>)? And what is in future lives (<s>sāṃparāyika</s>)? The acquisition of wealth through proper effort in crafts and occupational skills (<s>śilpasthānakarmasthāna</s>); the moderate enjoyment of those very acquired possessions; and of previously desired action whose ripening has matured,

body.text: yo dṛṣṭe dharme phalopabhogaḥ / dhyānavyāvartanakuśalasya ca bodhisattvasya dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihārārthaṃ dṛṣṭa eva ca dharme tatsanniśrayo na parārthaprasādhanārthaṃ dhyānasanniśrayaḥ / yacca dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇaṃ tathāgatabhūtasya ye ca laukikalokottarā dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇasaṃprāpakāḥ saṃskṛtā dharmāḥ / ayamucyate bodhisattvasya dṛṣṭadhārmikā eva svārthaḥ / yathā bodhisattvasyaivaṃ pareṣāmapi parārtho veditavyaḥ / ye sattvā bodhisattvavinītāḥ / tatra yā ca kāmadhātau bhogasaṃpatparatra yā cātmabhāvasaṃpat paratra / yā ca paratra dhyānārūpyopapattiḥ tasyāśca paratra bhogātmabhāvasaṃpado dhyānārūpyopapatteśca yā dṛṣṭe dharme sahaiva duḥkhena sahaiva daurmanasyena pratisaṃkhyāya pratisaṃkhyāya hetvāsevanā / ayaṃ sāṃparāyika eva bodhisattvasya svaparārtho veditavyaḥ / yā punardṛṣṭe dharme sahaiva sukhena sahaiva saumanasyena bhogātmabhāvasaṃpado hetvāsevanā / yā cehāhānabhāgīyā dhyānārūpyasamāpattiḥ / dṛṣṭadharmasāṃparāyikaḥ svaparārtho veditavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: the enjoyment of fruit in this present life; and for a <s>Bodhisattva</s> skilled in returning from meditative absorption (<s>dhyānavyāvartanakuśala</s>), the reliance on that for the purpose of pleasant abiding in this present life (<s>dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra</s>)—and indeed in this very life, the reliance on meditation is not for the purpose of accomplishing the benefit of others. And the <s>nirvāṇa</s> in this very life of one who has become a <s>Tathāgata</s>, and the conditioned <s>dharmas</s>, both mundane and supramundane, that lead to the attainment of <s>nirvāṇa</s> in this very life—this is called the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s own benefit in this present life. Just as for the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, so the benefit of others should be understood for those beings who are trained by the <s>Bodhisattva</s>. There, the prosperity of enjoyments in the desire-realm in future [lives], the prosperity of embodiment in future [lives], and the rebirth in the sphere of <s>dhyāna</s> and formless absorptions in future [lives]—and for that prosperity of enjoyments and embodiment in future [lives] and for that rebirth in the sphere of <s>dhyāna</s> and formless absorptions—the cultivation of causes in this present life, accompanied by pain and mental distress, through repeated deliberation—this should be understood as the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s benefit for self and others in future lives. And the cultivation of causes in this present life, accompanied by pleasure and mental joy, for the prosperity of enjoyments and embodiment; and the attainment of <s>dhyāna</s> and formless absorptions in this life that does not lead to decline—this should be understood as the benefit for self and others in both present and future lives.

body.text: ātyantikaḥ svaparārthaḥ katamaḥ / katamaścānātyantikaḥ / kāmadhātau bhogātmabhāvasaṃpattiḥ sahetuphalā laukikī ca pṛthagjanānāṃ śuddhiḥ sahetuphalā anātyantikaḥ svaparārthaḥ / sarvātyantakleśaprahāṇamāryāṣṭāṅgaśca mārgaḥ tadāśrayeṇa ca ye laukikāḥ kuśalā dharmāḥ pratilabdhāḥ / ayamucyate ātyantikaḥ svaparārthaḥ /
body.translated_text: What is the ultimate (<s>ātyantika</s>) benefit for self and others? And what is the non-ultimate (<s>anātyantika</s>)? The prosperity of enjoyments and embodiment in the desire-realm together with its cause and fruit, and the mundane purification of ordinary beings (<s>pṛthagjana</s>) together with its cause and fruit—this is the non-ultimate benefit for self and others. The complete abandonment of all afflictions (<s>sarvātyantakleśaprahāṇa</s>), the Noble Eightfold Path (<s>āryāṣṭāṅgamārga</s>), and the mundane wholesome <s>dharmas</s> obtained on the basis of that—this is called the ultimate benefit for self and others.

body.text: tatra tribhiḥ kāraṇairātyantikatā anātyantikatā ca veditavyā / svabhāvataḥ parihāṇitaḥ phalopabhoga parikṣayataśca / tatra svabhāvato nirvāṇamātyantikam / saṃskṛtaṃ sarvamevānātyantikam / āryāṣṭāṅgo mārgaḥ aparihāṇīyatvādaphalopa bhogāparikṣayādātyantikaḥ / tadanye kuśalasāstravā dharmāḥ parihāṇitaḥ phalopabhogaparikṣayataścānātyantikāḥ /
body.translated_text: There, the ultimate and non-ultimate nature should be understood by three criteria: by intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāvataḥ</s>), by the possibility of decline (<s>parihāṇitaḥ</s>), and by the exhaustion of the enjoyment of fruit (<s>phalopabhogaparikṣayataḥ</s>). There, by intrinsic nature, <s>nirvāṇa</s> is ultimate. All that is conditioned (<s>saṃskṛta</s>) is non-ultimate. The Noble Eightfold Path, because of its non-declining nature and because of the non-exhaustion of the enjoyment of its fruit, is ultimate. Other wholesome or instructive <s>dharmas</s>, due to the possibility of decline and due to the exhaustion of the enjoyment of their fruit, are non-ultimate.

body.text: ityayaṃ bodhisattvānāṃ daśavidhaḥ svaparārthaḥ samāsavistarataḥ yatra bodhisattvairyathāśakti yathābalaṃ śikṣitavyam nāta ūttari nāto bhūyaḥ / atīte 'pyadhvanyanāgate 'pi ye svaparārthe śikṣitavantaḥ śikṣiṣyante sarve te 'sminneva daśavidhe svaparārthe / nāta uttari nāto bhūyaḥ /
body.translated_text: Thus, this tenfold self-and-other benefit of <s>Bodhisattvas</s>, in brief and in detail, is that in which <s>Bodhisattvas</s> should train according to their capacity and power—there is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this. In the past and also in the future, those who have trained and will train in the benefit of self and others—all of them [train] in this very tenfold benefit of self and others. There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.

body.text: bodhisattvabhūmāvādhāre yogasthāne svaparārthapaṭalaṃ tṛtīyaṃ samāptam /
body.translated_text: In the <s>Bodhisattvabhūmi</s>, in the Foundation Section of Yoga (<s>Ādhārayogasthāna</s>), the third chapter on Self-and-Other Benefit (<s>Svaparārthapaṭala</s>) is completed.

body.text: tattvārthaḥ katamaḥ / samāsato dvividhaḥ / yathāvadbhāvikatāñca dharmāṇāmārabhya yā dharmāṇāṃ bhūtatā yāvadbhāvikatāñcārabhya yā dharmāṇāṃ sarvatā / iti bhūtatā sarvatā ca dharmāṇāṃ samastastattvārtho veditavyaḥ / sa punareva tattvārthaḥ prakārabhedataścaturvidhaḥ / lokaprasiddho yuktiprasiddhaḥ kleśāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocaro jñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocaraśca /
body.translated_text: What is the meaning of reality (<s>tattvārtha</s>)? In brief, it is twofold. With reference to the mode of being (<s>yathāvadbhāvikatā</s>) of <s>dharmas</s>—the true nature of <s>dharmas</s> (<s>bhūtatā</s>); and with reference to the extent of being (<s>yāvadbhāvikatā</s>)—the totality of <s>dharmas</s> (<s>sarvatā</s>). Thus, the true nature and the totality of <s>dharmas</s> together constitute the meaning of reality. That very meaning of reality, moreover, by differentiation of types, is fourfold: the conventionally established (<s>lokaprasiddha</s>), the established by reasoning (<s>yuktiprasiddha</s>), the domain of knowledge purified from the obscuration of afflictions (<s>kleśāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocara</s>), and the domain of knowledge purified from the obscuration of the knowable (<s>jñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocara</s>).

body.text: tatra laukikānāṃ sarveṣāṃ yasmin vastuni saṃketasaṃvṛtisaṃstavanāgamapraviṣṭayā buddhyā darśanatulyatā bhavati tadyathā pṛthivyāṃ pṛthivyaiveyaṃ nāgniriti / yathā pṛthivyāmevamagnāvapsu vāyau rūpeṣu śabdeṣu gandheṣu raseṣu spraṣṭavyeṣu bhojane pāne yāne vastre alaṅkāropavicāre bhāṇḍopaskare gandhamālyavilepane nṛtyagītavāditre āloke strīpuruṣaparicaryāyāṃ kṣetrāpaṇagṛhavastuni sukhaduḥkhe duḥkhamidaṃ na sukhaṃ sukhamidaṃ na duḥkhamiti / samāsata idamidaṃ nedam / evamidaṃ nānyatheti niścitādhimuktigocaro yadvastu sarveṣāmeva laukikānāṃ paraṃparāgatayā saṃjñayā svavikalpa-prasidvaṃ na cintayitvā tulayitvopaparīkṣyodgṛhītam / idamucyate lokaprasiddhatattvam /
body.translated_text: There, regarding all worldly people, that thing concerning which, through an understanding that has entered into conventional designation, customary expression, and tradition (<s>saṃketasaṃvṛtisaṃstavanāgama</s>), there is unanimity of perception—as for instance, regarding earth: 'This is earth, not fire.' Just as with earth, so with fire, water, wind, forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, food, drink, vehicles, clothing, ornaments and furnishings, vessels and utensils, perfumes, garlands and ointments, dancing, singing and music, light, the service of women and men, fields, shops, and dwelling-things, pleasure and pain: 'This is suffering, not pleasure; this is pleasure, not suffering.' In brief: 'This is this, not that; it is thus, not otherwise'—that thing which is the domain of firm conviction, established for all worldly people through the conventional designation handed down in succession, by their own conceptualizations, not taken up through thinking, weighing, or examining—this is called the conventionally established reality (<s>lokaprasiddha tattva</s>).

body.text: yuktiprasiddhatattvaṃ katamat / satāṃ yuktārthapaṇḍitānāṃ vicakṣaṇānāṃ tārkikāṇāṃ mīmāṃsakānāṃ tarkaparyāpannāyāṃ bhūmau sthitānāṃ svayaṃ prātibhānikyāṃ pārthagjanikyāṃ mīmāṃsānucaritāyāṃ pratyakṣamanumānamāptāgamaṃ pramāṇaṃ niśritya suvidita-suviniścitajñānagocara-jñeyaṃ vastūpapattisādhanayuktyā prasādhitaṃ vyavasthāpitam / idamucyate yuktiprasiddhaṃ tattvam /
body.translated_text: What is the reality established by reasoning (<s>yuktiprasiddha tattva</s>)? Among the learned, those who are skilled in reasoned meaning, wise, skilled in argumentation, examiners, standing on the ground of logical reasoning, relying on perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), inference (<s>anumāna</s>), and authoritative testimony (<s>āptāgama</s>) as means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), through their own self-arising, common-person's examination—that thing which is the object of well-ascertained and well-determined knowledge, established and determined by the reasoning of proof and fact (<s>vastūpapattisādhanayukti</s>)—this is called the reality established by reasoning.

body.text: kleśāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocarastattvaṃ katamat / sarvaśrāvakapratyekabuddhānāmanāsraveṇānāsravāvāhakena cānāsravapṛṣṭalabdhena ca laukikena jñānena yo gocaraviṣayaḥ / idamucyate kleśāvaraṇaviśudvijñānagocarastattvam / tenālambanena kleśāvaraṇāj
body.translated_text: What is the reality that is the domain of knowledge purified from the obscuration of afflictions (<s>kleśāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocara tattva</s>)? That which is the domain and object of the undefiled (<s>anāsrava</s>) knowledge, the knowledge leading to the undefiled, and the mundane knowledge obtained subsequent to the undefiled, of all <s>Śrāvakas</s> and <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s>—this is called the reality that is the domain of knowledge purified from the obscuration of afflictions. Through that object, from the obscuration of afflictions

body.text: jñānaṃ viśudhyati / anāvaraṇatve cāyatyāṃ santiṣṭhate / tasmātkleśāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocarastattvamityucyate /
body.translated_text: knowledge is purified. And in the future, it abides unobstructed. Therefore, it is called the reality that is the domain of knowledge purified from the obscuration of afflictions.

body.text: tatpunastatvaṃ katamat / catvāryāryaisatyāni duḥkhaṃ samudayo nirodho mārgaśca / ityetāni catvāryāryasatyāni pravicinvato 'bhisamāgacchato 'bhisamāgateṣu ca tajjñānamutpadyate / sa punaḥ satyābhisamayaḥ śrāvakapratyekabuddhānāṃ skandhamātramupalabhamānānāṃ skandhebhyaścānyamarthāntaramātmānamanupalabhamānānāṃ pratītyasamutpannasaṃskārodayavyayapratisaṃyuktayā prajñayā skandhavinirmuktapudgalābhāvadarśanābhyāsādutpadyate /
body.translated_text: What then is that reality (<s>tattva</s>)? The four noble truths (<s>āryasatya</s>): suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), origin (<s>samudaya</s>), cessation (<s>nirodha</s>), and the path (<s>mārga</s>). By investigating and comprehending these four noble truths, the corresponding knowledge arises. That comprehension of the truths (<s>satyābhisamaya</s>) arises for <s>Śrāvakas</s> and <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s>—who apprehend only the aggregates (<s>skandha</s>) and do not apprehend a self as something different and distinct from the aggregates—through the repeated practice of seeing the non-existence of a person apart from the aggregates, by means of the wisdom connected with the arising and passing away of conditioned formations that have arisen through dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>).

body.text: jñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocarastattvaṃ katamat / jñeye jñānasya pratighāta āvaraṇamityucyate / tena jñeyāvaraṇena vimuktasya jñānasya yo gocaraviṣayastajjñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocarastattvaṃ veditavyam /
body.translated_text: What is the reality that is the domain of knowledge purified from cognitive obscurations (<s>jñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhijñānagocarastattva</s>)? The obstruction of knowledge with respect to the knowable is called obscuration (<s>āvaraṇa</s>). The domain and object of knowledge that is freed from that cognitive obscuration—that is to be known as the reality that is the domain of knowledge purified from cognitive obscurations.

body.text: tatpunaḥ katamat / bodhisattvānāṃ buddhānāñca bhagavatāṃ dharmanairātmyapraveśāya praviṣṭena suviśuddhena ca sarvadharmāṇāṃ nirabhilāpyasvabhāvatāmārabhya prajñaptivāda svabhāvanirvikalpajñeyasamena jñānena yo gocaraviṣayaḥ sāsau paramā tathatā niruttarā jñeyaparyantagatā yasyāḥ sarva samyagdharmapravicayā nivartante nābhivartante /
body.translated_text: What then is that? The domain and object of the knowledge that has entered for the purpose of penetrating the selflessness of <s>dharmas</s> (<s>dharmanairātmya</s>) for <s>Bodhisattvas</s> and <s>Buddhas</s>, the <s>Bhagavāns</s>—the thoroughly purified, non-conceptual knowledge equal to the knowable, of the nature of designation, beginning with the inexpressible own-nature of all <s>dharmas</s>—that is the supreme <s>tathatā</s> (suchness), unsurpassed, having reached the limit of the knowable, from which all correct investigations of <s>dharma</s> turn back and do not proceed further.

body.text: tatpunastattvalakṣaṇaṃ vyavasthānataḥ advayaprabhāvitaṃ veditavyam / dvayamucyate bhāvaścābhāvaśca /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, the characteristic of reality, in terms of its determination, is to be known as established through non-duality (<s>advaya</s>). Duality is said to be existence (<s>bhāva</s>) and non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>).

body.text: tatra bhāvo yaḥ prajñaptivādasvabhāvo vyavasthāpitaḥ / tathaiva ca dīrghakālamabhiniviṣṭo lokena / sarvavikalpaprapañcamūlaṃ lokasya / tadyathā rūpamiti vā vedanā saṃjñā saṃskārā vijñānamiti vā / cakṣuriti vā srotraṃ ghrāṇaṃ jihvā kāyo mana iti vā / pṛthivīti vā āpastejo vāyuriti vā / rūpamiti vā śabdo gandho rasaḥ spraṣṭavyamiti vā / kuśalamiti vā akuśalamiti vā avyākṛtamiti vā / utpāda iti vā vyaya iti vā pratītyasamutpanna iti vā / atītamiti vā anātagamiti vā pratyutpannamiti vā / saṃskṛtamiti vā [asaṃskṛtamiti vā /] ayaṃ lokaḥ paro lokaḥ / ubhau sūryācandramasau / yadapi dṛṣṭaśrutamatavijñātaṃ prāptaṃ paryeṣitaṃ manasā 'nuvitarkitamanuvicāritamiti vā / antato yāvannirvāṇamiti vā / ityevaṃbhāgīyaḥ prajñaptivādanirūḍhaḥ svabhāvo dharmāṇāṃ lokasya bhāva ityucyate /
body.translated_text: Therein, 'existence' is the nature established through designation (<s>prajñaptivādasvabhāva</s>), in which the world has long been absorbed. [It is] the root of all conceptual proliferation (<s>vikalpaprapañca</s>) of the world. Namely: 'form' (<s>rūpa</s>), or 'feeling' (<s>vedanā</s>), 'perception' (<s>saṃjñā</s>), 'formations' (<s>saṃskāra</s>), 'consciousness' (<s>vijñāna</s>); or 'eye' (<s>cakṣus</s>), 'ear' (<s>śrotra</s>), 'nose' (<s>ghrāṇa</s>), 'tongue' (<s>jihvā</s>), 'body' (<s>kāya</s>), 'mind' (<s>manas</s>); or 'earth' (<s>pṛthivī</s>), 'water' (<s>āpas</s>), 'fire' (<s>tejas</s>), 'wind' (<s>vāyu</s>); or 'form' (<s>rūpa</s>), 'sound' (<s>śabda</s>), 'smell' (<s>gandha</s>), 'taste' (<s>rasa</s>), 'touch' (<s>spraṣṭavya</s>); or 'wholesome' (<s>kuśala</s>), 'unwholesome' (<s>akuśala</s>), 'indeterminate' (<s>avyākṛta</s>); or 'arising' (<s>utpāda</s>), 'cessation' (<s>vyaya</s>), 'dependently arisen' (<s>pratītyasamutpanna</s>); or 'past' (<s>atīta</s>), 'future' (<s>anāgata</s>), 'present' (<s>pratyutpanna</s>); or 'conditioned' (<s>saṃskṛta</s>), ['unconditioned' (<s>asaṃskṛta</s>);] 'this world,' 'the other world'; 'both sun and moon'; also 'what is seen, heard, thought, cognized, attained, sought, mentally investigated, and reflected upon'; down to '<s>nirvāṇa</s>.' Such and similar is the nature of <s>dharmas</s> established through designation—this is called 'existence' for the world.

body.text: tatrābhāvo yā asyaiva rūpamiti prajñaptivādasya yāvadantato nirvāṇamiti prajñaptivādasya nirvastukatā nirnimittatā prajñaptivādāśrayasya sarveṇa sarvaṃ nāstikatā asaṃvidyamānatā yāmāśritya prajñaptivādaḥ pravartate / ayamucyate 'bhāvaḥ /
body.translated_text: Therein, 'non-existence' is the substancelessness, signlessness—the complete non-existence, the non-finding—of the very basis of designation, beginning with the designation 'form' down to the designation '<s>nirvāṇa</s>,' upon which designation operates. This is called 'non-existence.'

body.text: yatpunaḥ pūrvakeṇa ca bhāvenānena cābhāvena ubhābhyāṃ bhāvābhāvābhyāṃ vinirmuktaṃ dharmalakṣaṇasaṃgṛhītaṃ vastu / tadadvayaṃm yadadvayam tanmadhyamā-pratipadantadvayavarjitam / niruttaretyucyate / tasmiṃśca tattve buddhānāṃ bhagavatāṃ suviśuddhaṃ jñānaṃ veditavyam / bodhisattvānāṃ punaḥ śikṣāmārgaprabhāvitaṃ tatra jñānaṃ veditavyam /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, that which is freed from both the former 'existence' and this 'non-existence'—from both existence and non-existence—the entity encompassed by the characteristic of <s>dharma</s>: that is non-duality (<s>advaya</s>). What is non-dual is the middle path (<s>madhyamā pratipad</s>), free from both extremes; it is called 'unsurpassed.' And regarding that reality, the knowledge of the <s>Buddhas</s>, the <s>Bhagavāns</s>, is to be known as thoroughly purified. The knowledge of <s>Bodhisattvas</s>, however, is to be known as established through the path of training.

body.text: sā ca prajñā mahānupāyo bodhisattvasyānuttarāyāḥ samyaksaṃbodheḥ prāptaye / taktasya heto / tathā hi bodhisattvastena śūnyatādhimokṣeṇa tāsu tāsu jātiṣu prayujyamānaḥ sattveṣu buddhadharmaparipākāya saṃsāre saṃsaran tañca saṃsāraṃ yathābhūtaṃ parijānāti / na ca punastasmātsaṃsārādanityādibhirākārairmānasamudvejayati / sa
body.translated_text: And that wisdom is the great skillful means (<s>mahānupāya</s>) of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> for attaining unsurpassed perfect awakening. For what reason? For the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, applying himself through that conviction in emptiness (<s>śūnyatādhimokṣa</s>) in various births, transmigrating in <s>saṃsāra</s> for the sake of ripening <s>Buddha</s>-qualities in beings, comprehends that <s>saṃsāra</s> as it truly is. And yet he does not generate revulsion from that <s>saṃsāra</s> through aspects such as impermanence.

body.text: cetsaṃsāraṃ yathābhūtaṃ na parijānīyānnaśaknuyādrāgadveṣamohādikāt sarvasaṃkleśāccittamadhyupekṣitum / anadhyupekṣamāṇaścasaṃkliṣṭacittaḥ saṃsāre saṃsaret saṃkliṣṭacittaḥ saṃsarannaiva buddhadharmān paripācayennāpi sattvān / sa cet punaranityādibhirākāraiḥ saṃsārānmānasamudvejayedevaṃ sati bodhisattvo laghu ladhveva parinirvāyāt / laghu ladhveva ca parinirvāyan bodhisattva evamapi naiva buddhadharmānnaiva sattvān paripācayet / kutaḥ punaranuttarāṃ samyaksambodhimabhisaṃbhotsyate / tenaiva ca śūnyatādhimokṣeṇa bodhisattvaḥ prayujyamānaḥ na nirvāṇāduttrasyati nāpi nirvāṇaṃ prārthayate / sa cedvodhisattvo nirvāṇāduttrasyet paratra nirvāṇasaṃbhāro 'sya na paripūryeta yathāpi ca taduttrastamānasatvānnirvāṇe 'nanuśaṃsadarśinastadgataguṇadarśanaprasādādhimuktivivarjitasya bodhisattvasya / sa cetpunarbodhisattvo nirvāṇo prārthanābahulavihārī bhavedāśveva parinirvāyāt / āśu parinirvāyam naiva buddhadharmānna sattvān paripācayet / tatra yā ca saṃsāraṃ yathābhūtamaparijānataḥ saṃkliṣṭacittasya saṃsārasaṃsṛtiḥ / yā ca saṃsārādudvignamānasasyāśunirvṛtiḥ / yā ca nirvāṇāduttrastamānasasya tatsaṃbhārāparipūriḥ / yā ca nirvāṇaprārthanābahulavihāriṇa
body.translated_text: If he did not comprehend <s>saṃsāra</s> as it truly is, he would be unable to be indifferent in mind toward all defilement arising from desire, hatred, delusion, and so forth. Being unable to be indifferent, with a defiled mind transmigrating in <s>saṃsāra</s>, with a defiled mind while transmigrating, he would neither ripen <s>Buddha</s>-qualities nor beings. If, on the other hand, he were to generate revulsion from <s>saṃsāra</s> through aspects such as impermanence, then the <s>Bodhisattva</s> would quickly pass into <s>parinirvāṇa</s>. Quickly passing into <s>parinirvāṇa</s>, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> would likewise neither ripen <s>Buddha</s>-qualities nor beings. How then would he fully awaken to unsurpassed perfect awakening? And through that very conviction in emptiness, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, applying himself, is neither terrified of <s>nirvāṇa</s> nor does he aspire to <s>nirvāṇa</s>. If the <s>Bodhisattva</s> were terrified of <s>nirvāṇa</s>, the accumulation for <s>nirvāṇa</s> would not be fulfilled for him, inasmuch as one with a terrified mind would not perceive the benefits of <s>nirvāṇa</s> and would be devoid of faith and conviction in seeing the qualities therein. If, on the other hand, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> were to dwell excessively in aspiration for <s>nirvāṇa</s>, he would quickly pass into <s>parinirvāṇa</s>. Quickly passing into <s>parinirvāṇa</s>, he would neither ripen <s>Buddha</s>-qualities nor beings. There, the transmigration in <s>saṃsāra</s> of one with a defiled mind who does not comprehend <s>saṃsāra</s> as it truly is; the quick cessation of one whose mind is agitated by <s>saṃsāra</s>; the non-fulfillment of the accumulation of one whose mind is terrified of <s>nirvāṇa</s>; the quick cessation of one who dwells excessively in aspiration for <s>nirvāṇa</s>—

body.text: āśu parinirvṛtiḥ ayamanupāyo bodhisattvasya veditavyo 'nuttarāyāḥ samyaksaṃbodheḥ / yā punaḥ saṃsāraṃ yathābhūtaṃ parijānato 'saṃkliṣṭacittasya saṃsārasaṃsṛtiḥ / yā ca saṃsārādanityādibhirākārairanudvignamānasasyānāśunirvṛtiḥ / yā ca nirvāṇādanuttrastamānasasya tatsaṃbhāraparipūriryā ca nirvāṇe guṇānuśaṃsadarśino na cātyarthamutkaṇṭhāprāptasyāśu nirvṛtiḥ / ayaṃ bodhisattvasya mahānupāyo 'nuttarāyāḥ samyaksambodheranu prāptaye / sa cāyamupāyastasmin paramaśūnyatādhimokṣe sanniśritaḥ /
body.translated_text: this is to be known as the non-skillful means of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> for unsurpassed perfect awakening. The transmigration in <s>saṃsāra</s> of one with an undefiled mind who comprehends <s>saṃsāra</s> as it truly is; the non-quick cessation of one whose mind is not agitated by <s>saṃsāra</s> through aspects such as impermanence; the fulfillment of the accumulation of one whose mind is not terrified of <s>nirvāṇa</s>; and the non-quick cessation of one who perceives the qualities and benefits of <s>nirvāṇa</s> yet does not become excessively eager—this is the great skillful means of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> for the attainment of unsurpassed perfect awakening. And this skillful means is grounded in that supreme conviction in emptiness.

body.text: tasmātsā paramanśūyatādhimokṣabhāvanā bodhisattvasya śikṣāmārgasaṃgṛhīto mahānupāya ityucyate yaduta tathāgatajñānādhigamāya / sa khalu bodhisattvastena dūrānupraviṣṭe na dharmanairātmyajñānena nirabhilāpyasvabhāvatāṃ sarvadharmāṇāṃ yathābhūtaṃ viditvā na kiñcidvikalpayati nānyatra vastumātraṃ gṛhṇāti tathatāmātram / na cāsyaivaṃ bhavati vastumātraṃ vā etattathatāmātraṃ caiti / arthe tu sa bodhisattvaścarati / arthe parame caran sarvadharmāṃstayā tathatayā samasamān yathābhūtaṃ prajñayā paśyati / sarvatra ca samadarśī samacittaḥ san paramāmupekṣāṃ pratilabhate / yāmāśritya sarvavidyāsthānakauśaleṣu prayujyamāno bodhisattvaḥ sarvapariśramaiḥ sarvaduḥkhopanipātaiḥ na nivartate / kṣiprañcāklāntakāyaḥ aklāntacittaḥ tatkauśalaṃ samudāyanayati / mahāsmṛtibalādhānaprāptaśca bhavati / na ca tena kauśalenonnatiṃ gacchati / na ca pareṣāmācāryamuṣṭiṃ karoti / sarvakauśaleṣu cāsaṃlīnacitto bhavati / utsāhavānavyāhatagatiśca bhavati / dṛḍhasannāhaprayogaḥ yathā yathā saṃsāre saṃsaran duḥkhaviśeṣaṃ labhate tathā tathotsāhaṃ bardhayatyanuttarāyāṃ samyaksaṃbodhau / yathā yathā samucchrayaviśeṣamadhigacchati tathā tathānirmānataro bhavati sattvānāmantike / yathā yathā jñānaviśeṣamadhigacchati tathā tathā bhūyasyā mātrayā paropārambhavivādaprakīrṇalapitākleśopakleśebhyaśca vṛttaskha litasamudācārebhyaḥ parijñāya parijñāya cittamadhyupekṣate / yathā yathā guṇairvi[va]rdhate tathā tathā praticchannakalyāṇo bhavati / na parato jñātuṃ samanveṣate na lābha satkāram / imā
body.translated_text: Therefore, that cultivation of supreme conviction in emptiness (<s>śūnyatādhimokṣa</s>), encompassed by the training-path of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, is called the great skillful means—namely, for the attainment of <s>Tathāgata</s>-knowledge. That <s>Bodhisattva</s>, having truly known through the deeply penetrating knowledge of the selflessness of <s>dharmas</s> the inexpressible own-nature of all <s>dharmas</s>, does not conceptualize anything, nor does he grasp anything other than the mere entity, the mere <s>tathatā</s> (suchness). Nor does the thought occur to him: 'This is merely an entity' or 'This is merely suchness.' But that <s>Bodhisattva</s> acts in accordance with meaning. Acting in accordance with the supreme meaning, he sees with wisdom, as it truly is, all <s>dharmas</s> as equal by that <s>tathatā</s>. And being impartial in vision everywhere, with an equal mind, he attains supreme equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>). Relying on this, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, applying himself to skill in all fields of knowledge, is not turned back by any hardship or any assault of suffering. Quickly, with an unfatigued body and unfatigued mind, he accomplishes that skill. Having attained the power of great mindfulness, he does not become conceited by that skill, nor does he hold back a teacher's fist from others. In all skills he maintains an uncontracted mind. He is endowed with enthusiasm and of unobstructed progress. With firm preparation and exertion, the more he transmigrates in <s>saṃsāra</s> and encounters special sufferings, the more he increases his enthusiasm for unsurpassed perfect awakening. The more he attains special eminence, the more humble he becomes before beings. The more he attains special knowledge, the more, to an even greater extent, he comprehends and becomes indifferent in mind toward others' accusations, disputes, idle talk, afflictions, and secondary defilements, and toward lapses of conduct. The more he grows in qualities, the more he conceals his virtues. He does not seek to be known by others, nor [does he seek] gain, honor, or fame.

body.text: evaṃbhāgīyā bahavo 'nuśaṃsā bhavanti bodhisattvasya bodhipakṣyā bodhyanukūlāstajjñānasanniśritasya / tasmād ye kecidbodhimanuprāptavanto ye ca kecitprāpsyanti ye ca prāpnuvanti sarve ta etadeva jñānaṃ niśritya nānyannyūnaṃ prativiśiṣṭaṃ vā / evaṃ niṣprapañcanayārūḍho bodhisattva evaṃ caṃ bahvanuśaṃsa ātmanaśca buddhadharmaparipākāya pareṣāñca yānatrayadharmaparipākāya samyak pratipanno bhavati / evañca punaḥ samyak pratipanno bhavati / bhogeṣvātmabhāve ca nistṛṣṇo bhavati / nistṛṣṇatāyāñca śikṣate sattveṣu bhogātmabhāvaparityāgāya sattvānāmevārthāya / saṃvṛtaśca bhavati susaṃvṛtaḥ / kāyena vācā sambareṇa ca śikṣate prakṛtyā pāpārucitāyai prakṛtibhadrakalyāṇatāyai ca / kṣamo bhavati parataḥ sarvopatāpakipratipattīnām / kṣamitvaṃ ca śikṣate mandakrodhatāyai ca a-paropatāpanatāyai ca / sarvavidyāsthāneṣu cābhiyukto bhavati kuśalaśca sattvānāṃ vicikitsāprahāṇāyānugrahopasaṃhārāya ca ātmanaśca sarvajñatvahetuparigrahāya / adhyātmasthitacittaśca bhavati susamāhitacittaḥ / cittasthitaye ca śikṣate caturbrāhmavihārapariśodhanatāyai pañcābhijñāvikrīḍanatāyai ca sattvakṛtyānuṣṭhānatāyai sarvakauśalyābhiyogajakleśa-vinodanatāyai ca / vicakṣaṇaśca bhavati paramatattvajñaḥ / paramatattvajñatāyai ca śikṣate mahāyāne cāyatyāmātmanaḥ parinirvāṇāya / sa khalu bodhisattva evaṃ samyakprayukto guṇavatsu sattveṣu pūjālābhasatkāreṇa pratyupasthito bhavati / doṣavatsu sattveṣu parameṇa kāruṇyacittenānukampācittena pratyupasthito bhavati / yathāśaktyā ca yathābalaṃ doṣaprahāṇāyaiṣāṃ prayujyate / apakāriṣu sattveṣu maitracittatayā pratyupasthito bhavati / yathāśaktyā ca yathābalam aśaṭho bhūtvā amāyāvī teṣāṃ hitasukhamupasaṃharati / teṣāmapakāriṇāṃ svenāśayaprayogadoṣeṇa vairacittatāyāḥ prahāṇārthamupakāriṣu sattveṣu kṛtajñatayā tulyādhikena pratyupakāreṇa pratyupasthito bhavati / āśāñca dhārmikī paripūrayatyasya yathāśaktyā yathābalam / apratibalo 'pi ca yācitaḥ san teṣu teṣu kṛtyakaraṇīyeṣvādaraṃ vyāyāmamupadarśayati na sakṛdeva nirākaroti / kathamayaṃ saṃjñāpyetā 'śakto 'haṃ nākarttukāma iti / ityayamevaṃbhāgīyo bodhisattvasya niṣprapañcanayārūḍhasya paramatattvajñāna-sanniśritasya samyakprayogo veditavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: Such and similar are the many benefits of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> that are conducive to awakening and favorable to awakening, for one who relies on that knowledge. Therefore, all who have attained awakening, who will attain it, and who are attaining it—all of them do so relying on this very knowledge, not on anything else, whether inferior or superior. Thus, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> who has ascended to the approach free from conceptual proliferation (<s>niṣprapañcanaya</s>), having such many benefits, is rightly engaged for the ripening of <s>Buddha</s>-qualities for himself and for the ripening of beings in the <s>Dharma</s> of the three vehicles. And he is rightly engaged in this way: he becomes free from craving toward possessions and his own person. He trains in freedom from craving for the sake of relinquishing possessions and his own person for the welfare of beings. He is restrained, well-restrained. He trains in body, speech, and conduct for natural aversion to evil and for natural auspiciousness and wholesomeness. He is patient with all harmful and adverse actions from others. He trains in patience for mildness of anger and for not causing harm to others. He is devoted to all fields of knowledge and skilled in removing the doubts of beings, in providing assistance, and in gathering the causes of omniscience for himself. He is one whose mind abides inwardly, of well-concentrated mind. He trains in mental stability for the purification of the four <s>brahmavihāras</s> (divine abidings), for playing with the five superknowledges (<s>abhijñā</s>), for carrying out duties toward beings, for dispelling afflictions arising from the application of all skills. He is discerning, a knower of supreme reality. He trains in knowledge of supreme reality for his own final <s>parinirvāṇa</s> in the future in the <s>Mahāyāna</s>. That <s>Bodhisattva</s>, rightly engaged in this way, is present to beings endowed with qualities with offerings, gain, and honor. To beings endowed with faults, he is present with supreme compassionate and sympathetic mind. And he exerts himself according to his ability and power for the abandonment of their faults. To beings who have done him harm, he is present with a mind of friendliness. According to his ability and power, being sincere and without deceit, he provides them with welfare and happiness. For the sake of abandoning the hostile mind of those who have done him harm—[arising] through their own faults of intention and action—he is present to beings who have done him good with gratitude and with an equal or greater reciprocation. He fulfills their righteous hopes according to his ability and power. Even when unable, if asked about various duties and tasks, he shows regard and effort, and does not refuse outright, [thinking:] 'How can this person be made to understand that I am unable, not unwilling?' This is the right engagement of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> who has ascended to the approach free from conceptual proliferation, relying on the knowledge of supreme reality.

body.text: tatra kayā yuktyā nirabhilāpyasvabhāvatā sarvadharmāṇāṃ pratyavagantavyā / yeyaṃ svalakṣaṇaprajñaptirdharmāṇāṃ yaduta rūpamiti vā vedaneti vā pūrvavadantato yāvannirvāṇamiti vā prajñaptimātrameva tadveditavyam / na svabhāvo nāpi ca tadvinirmuktastadanyo vāggocaro vāgaviṣayaḥ / evaṃ sati na svabhāvo dharmāṇāṃ tathā vidyate yathābhilapyate / na ca punaḥ sarveṃṇa sarvaṃ na vidyate / sa punarevamavidyamāno na ca sarveṇa sarvamavidyamānaḥ / kathaṃ vidyate / asadbhū tasamāropāsaṃgrāhavivarjitaśca bhūtāpavādāsaṃgrāhavivarjitaśca vidyate / sa punaḥ pāramārthikaḥ svabhāvaḥ sarvadharmāṇāṃ nirvikalpasyaiva jñānasya gocaro veditavyaḥ / sa cetpunaryathaivābhilāpo yeṣu dharmeṣu yasminvastuni pravartate tadātmakāste dharmā vā tadvastu syāt / evaṃ sati bahuvidhā bahavaḥ svabhāvā ekasya dharmasyaikasya vastuno bhaveyuḥ / tat kasya hetoḥ / tathā hyekasmindharme ekasminvastuni bahuvidhā bahavo bahubhirabhilāpaiḥ prajñaptaya upacārāḥ kriyante / na ca bahuvidhānāñca bahūnāṃ prajñaptivādānāṃ niyamaḥ kaścidupalabhyate / yadanyatamena prajñaptivādenaikena tasya dharmasya tasya vastunaḥ tādātmyaṃ tanmayatā tatsvabhāvatā syānnānyairavaśiṣṭaiḥ prajñaptivādaiḥ / tasmātsakalavikalaiḥ sarvaprajñaptivādaiḥ sarvadharmāṇāṃ sarvavastūnāṃ nāsti tādātmyaṃ nāsti tanmayatā nāsti tatsvabhāvatā / api ca sa cedrūpādayo dharmā yathāpūrvanirdiṣṭāḥ prajñaptivādasvabhāvā bhaveyuḥ / evaṃ sati pūrva tāvadvastu paścāttatra chandataḥ prajñaptivādopacāraḥ / prākprajñaptivādopacārādakṛte prajñaptivādopacāre sa dharmastadvastu niḥsvabhāva eva syāt / sati niḥsvabhāvatve nirvastukaḥ prajñaptivādo na yujyate / prajñaptivādopacāre cāsati prajñaptivādasvabhāvatā dharmasya vastuno na yujyeta / sa cetpunaḥ pūrvameva prajñaptivādopacārādakṛte prajñaptivādopacāre sa dharmastadvastu tadātmakaṃ syāt / evaṃ sati vinā tena rūpamiti prajñaptivādopacāreṇa rūpasaṃjñake dharme rūpasaṃjñake vastuni rūpabuddhiḥ pravarteta / na ca pravartate / tadanena kāraṇonānayā yuktyā nirabhilāpyaḥ svabhāvaḥ sarvadharmāṇāṃ pratyavagantavyaḥ / yathārūpamevaṃ vedanādayo yathānirdiṣṭā dharmā antato yāvannirvāṇaparyantā veditavyāḥ /
body.translated_text: There, by what reasoning is the inexpressible own-nature (<s>nirabhilāpyasvabhāvatā</s>) of all <s>dharmas</s> to be comprehended? The designation of the individual characteristics of <s>dharmas</s> — such as 'form,' 'feeling,' and so on as previously [described], up to '<s>nirvāṇa</s>' — all of that is to be understood as mere designation (<s>prajñaptimātra</s>). It is not [their] own-nature, nor is there any verbal object or domain of speech that is separate from it. This being so, the own-nature of <s>dharmas</s> does not exist as it is expressed. And yet it is not the case that absolutely nothing exists at all. Being thus non-existent [as expressed], and yet not completely non-existent — how does it exist? It exists as free from the inclusion in unreal superimposition (<s>asadbhūtasamāropa</s>) and as free from the inclusion in the denial of what is real (<s>bhūtāpavāda</s>). That ultimate own-nature (<s>pāramārthikasvabhāva</s>) of all <s>dharmas</s> is to be understood as the domain only of non-conceptual knowledge (<s>nirvikalpajñāna</s>). Now, if the <s>dharmas</s> and the object in which verbal expression operates were identical in nature with those very expressions, then there would be many and various own-natures for a single <s>dharma</s>, for a single object. For what reason? Because with regard to a single <s>dharma</s>, a single object, many and various designations and metaphorical applications are made through many verbal expressions. And no fixed rule is found among the many and various designative statements such that by one particular designative statement alone, that <s>dharma</s> or that object would have identity, consist of it, or have it as its own-nature, and not by other remaining designative statements. Therefore, through all designative statements, with all their divisions, there is no identity, no consisting of, no having-as-own-nature of all <s>dharmas</s> and all objects. Furthermore, if <s>dharmas</s> such as form and the rest, as previously indicated, were to have the nature of designative statements, then the object would first exist, and afterward a designative metaphorical application would be made to it at will. Prior to the designative metaphorical application, when no such application has been made, that <s>dharma</s>, that object, would indeed be without own-nature. Given its lack of own-nature, an objectless designative statement would not be appropriate. And without a designative metaphorical application, the designative-statement-own-nature of the <s>dharma</s> or object would not be appropriate. Furthermore, if prior to any designative metaphorical application, when no such application has been made, that <s>dharma</s>, that object, were already identical with it, then without the designative metaphorical application of 'form,' the cognition of form would operate in a <s>dharma</s> designated as form, in an object designated as form — but it does not operate thus. For this reason, by this reasoning, the inexpressible own-nature of all <s>dharmas</s> is to be comprehended. Just as with form, so with feeling and the rest, as indicated, up to and including <s>nirvāṇa</s>, this is to be understood.

body.text: dvāvimāvasmāddharmavinayātpranaṣṭau veditavyau / yaśca rūpādīnāṃ dharmāṇāṃ rūpādikasya vastunaḥ prajñaptivādasvabhāvaṃ svalakṣaṇamasadbhūtasamāropato 'bhiniviśate / yaścāpi prajñaptivādanimittādhiṣṭhānaṃ prajñaptivādanimittasanniśrayaṃ
body.translated_text: Two [types of persons] are to be understood as lost from this <s>Dharma</s>-Vinaya: one who, through unreal superimposition, clings to the own-characteristic of <s>dharmas</s> such as form and so forth, of an object designated as form and so forth, as having the own-nature of a designative statement; and one who, relying on the sign of a designative statement as the foundation and support of the sign of a designative statement,

body.text: nirabhilāpyātmakatayā paramārthasadbhūtaṃ vastvapadamāno nāśayati sarveṇa sarvaṃ nāstīti / asadbhūtasamārope tāvadye doṣāste pūrvameva nirūpitā uttānā viśaditāḥ prakāśitāḥ / yairdoṣai rūpādike vastunayasadbhūtasamāropātpranaṣṭo bhavatyasmāddharmavinayāditi veditavyaḥ / yathā punā rūpādikeṣu dharmeṣuvastumātramapyapavadamānaḥ sarvavaināśikaḥ pranaṣṭo bhavatyasmāddharmavinayāt tathā vakṣyāmi rūpādīnāṃ dharmānāṃ vastumātramapavadato naiva tattvaṃ nāpi prajñaptistadubhayametanna yujyate / tadyathā satsu rūpādiṣu skandheṣu pudgalaprajñaptiryujyate / nāsatsu / nirvastukāpudgalaprajñaptiḥ / evaṃ sati rūpādīnāṃ dharmāṇāṃ vastumātre [sa] rūpādidharmaprajñaptivādopacāro yujyate / nāsati / nirvastukaḥ prajñaptivādopacāraḥ / tatra prajñaptervastu nāstīti niradhiṣṭhānā prajñaptirapi nāsti / ato ya ekatyā durvijñeyān sūtrāntānmahāyānapratisaṃyuktān gambhīrān śūnyatāpratisaṃyuktānābhiprāyikārthanirūpitān śrutvā yathābhūtaṃ bhāṣitasyārthamavijñāyāyoniśo vikalpyāyogavihitena tarkamātrakeṇaivaṃ dṛṣṭayo bhavantyevaṃvādinaḥ / prajñaptimātrameva sarvametacca tattvam / yaścaivaṃ paśyati sa samyak paśyatīti / teṣāṃ prajñaptyadhiṣṭhānasya vastumātrasyābhāvātsaiva prajñaptiḥ sarveṇa sarvaṃ na bhavati / kutaḥ punaḥ prajñaptimātraṃ tattvaṃ bhaviṣyatīti / tadanena paryāyeṇa taistattvamapi prajñaptirapi tadubhayamapyapavāditaṃ bhavati / prajñaptitattvāpavādācca pradhāno nāstiko veditavyaḥ / sa evaṃ nāṣṭikaḥ sannakathyo bhavatyasaṃvāsyo bhavati vijñānāṃ sabrahmacāriṇām / sa ātmānamapi vipādayati / loko 'pi yo 'sya dṛṣṭyanumata āpādyate / idañca sandhāyoktaṃ bhagavatā- varamihaikatyasya pudgaladṛṣṭirna tvevaikatyasya durgṛhītā śūnyateti / taktasya hetoḥ / pudgaladṛṣṭiko janturjñeye kevalaṃ muhyennatu sarva jñeyamapavadeta / na tato nidānamapāyeṣūpapadyeta / nāpi dharmārthikaṃ duḥkhavimokṣārthikañca paraṃ visaṃvādayenna vipralambhayet / dharme
body.translated_text: by denying [that any] object truly exists in the ultimate sense as having an inexpressible nature, destroys it [thinking:] 'Nothing whatsoever exists at all.' As for the faults in unreal superimposition, those have already been analyzed, explained, elucidated, and made clear. Through those faults, one who [holds to] unreal superimposition regarding objects such as form and so forth is to be understood as lost from this <s>Dharma</s>-Vinaya. As for how one who denies even the mere object among <s>dharmas</s> such as form and so forth, being a complete nihilist, is lost from this <s>Dharma</s>-Vinaya — I shall now explain: For one who denies even the mere object of <s>dharmas</s> such as form and so forth, neither reality (<s>tattva</s>) nor designation (<s>prajñapti</s>) is appropriate; both together are not appropriate. Just as when the aggregates (<s>skandha</s>) such as form exist, the designation of 'person' (<s>pudgala</s>) is appropriate — not when they do not exist — and without an object, the designation of 'person' [is not appropriate]; so too, when the mere object of <s>dharmas</s> such as form exists, the designative metaphorical application of <s>dharmas</s> such as form is appropriate — not when it does not exist — and without an object, the designative metaphorical application [is not appropriate]. There, when the object of designation does not exist, the designation itself, being without a foundation, also does not exist. Therefore, certain ones, having heard difficult-to-understand <s>sūtras</s> connected with the <s>Mahāyāna</s>, profound, connected with emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>), whose meaning is set forth as intentional (<s>ābhiprāyika</s>), and not knowing the true meaning of what was spoken, improperly conceptualizing, through mere speculation unskillfully engaged — they come to have such views, become such advocates: 'All this is mere designation, and that indeed is reality. One who sees thus sees correctly.' For them, since the mere object that is the foundation of designation does not exist, that very designation itself does not exist at all. How then could mere designation be reality? Therefore, by this approach, reality, designation, and both together are denied by them. And from the denial of both reality and designation, one is to be understood as a thorough nihilist. Being thus a nihilist, one is unspeakable and unfit for association among wise fellow practitioners of the holy life. One ruins oneself and also the world that is led by his views. And with this in mind, the <s>Bhagavān</s> has said: 'Better, indeed, is the view of a person (<s>pudgaladṛṣṭi</s>) in a certain individual, than the wrongly grasped emptiness in another.' For what reason? One with the view of a person would merely be confused about the knowable, but would not deny all that is knowable. He would not on that account be reborn in the lower realms. Nor would he deceive and mislead one who is seeking the <s>Dharma</s> and seeking liberation from suffering. He would establish [the other] in the <s>Dharma</s>

body.text: satye ca pratiṣṭhāpayet / [na ca śaithiliko bhavecchikṣāpadeṣu / durgṛhītayā punaḥ śūnyatayā jñeye vastuni muhyet / apyapavadet jñeyaṃ sarvam / tannidānaṃ cāpāyeṣūpapadyate / dhārmikaṃ ca duḥkhavimokṣārthikaṃ paraṃ vipādayet / śaithilikaśca syācchikṣāpadeṣu / evaṃbhūtaṃ vastu apavadamānaḥ praṇaṣṭo bhavatyasmād dharmavinayāt /
body.translated_text: and in truth. [And he would not be lax in the training precepts. But through wrongly grasped emptiness, one would be confused about the knowable objects. One would even deny all that is knowable. On that account, one would be reborn in the lower realms. One would mislead and ruin one who is righteous and seeking liberation from suffering. And one would be lax in the training precepts. One who denies such an object as this is lost from this <s>Dharma</s>-Vinaya.
