body.text: kathañca bodhisattvaścatvāryapramāṇāni bhāvayati / maitrīṃ karuṇāṃ muditāmupekṣām / iha bodhisattvaḥ samāsatastrividhāni catvāryapramāṇāni bhāvayati / sattvālambanāni dharmālambanānyanālambanāni ca / yadbodhisattvastriṣu rāśiṣu sarvasattvānavasthāpya sukhitān duḥkhitān aduḥkhitāsukhitān sattvān sukhakāmānadhikṛtya sukhopasaṃhārādhyāśayagatena maitreṇa cetasā daśadiśaḥ spharitvā sattvādhimokṣeṇa viharati / iyamasya sattvālambanā maitrī veditavyā / yatpunaḥ dharmamātrasaṃjñī dharmamātre sattvopacāramāśayataḥ saṃpaśyaṃstāmeva maitrīṃ bhāvayati / iyamasya dharmālambanā maitrī veditavyā / yatpunardharmānapyavikalpayaṃstāmeva maitrīṃ bhāvayati / iyamasyānālambanā maitrī veditavyā / yathā sattvālambanā dharmālambanā 'nālambanā maitrī evaṃ karuṇā muditopekṣā api veditavyā / tatra bodhisattvo duḥkhitān sattvānārabhya duḥkhāpanayanādhyāśayo daśasu dikṣu karuṇāsahagataṃ cittaṃ bhāvayati / sāsya karuṇā / sukhitānvā punaḥ sattvānārabhya sukhānumodanādhyāśayo dasaśu dikṣu muditāsahagataṃ cittaṃ bhāvayati / sāsya muditā / sa teṣāmeva trividhānāṃ sattvānāmaduḥkhāsukhitānā duḥkhitānāṃ sukhitānāñca yathākramaṃ mohadveṣarāgakleśavivekādhyāśayo daśasu dikṣūpekṣāsahagataṃ cittaṃ bhāvayati / iyamasyopekṣā / tatra yāni bodhisattvasya maitryādīnyapramāṇāni sattvālambanāni tānyanyatīrthya sādhāraṇāni veditavyāni / yāni punardharmālambanāni tāni śrāvakapratyekabuddhasādhāraṇāni na tvanyatīrthyasādhāraṇāni veditavyāni / yāni tu bodhisattvasyānālambanānyapramāṇāni tāni sarvatīrthya-śrāvakapratyekabuddhāsādhāraṇāni veditavyāni / tatra bodhisattvasya trīṇyapramāṇāni sukhādhyāśayasaṃgṛhītāni veditavyāni / maitrī karuṇā muditā ca / ekama pramāṇaṃ hitādhyāśayasaṃgṛhītaṃ veditavyaṃ yaduta upekṣā / sarvāṇi caitānyapramāṇāni bodhisattvasyānukampetyucyate / tasmāttaiḥ samanvāgatā bodhisattvā anukampakā ityucyante /
body.translated_text: And how does a <s>Bodhisattva</s> cultivate the four immeasurables (<s>apramāṇa</s>)—loving-kindness (<s>maitrī</s>), compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>), sympathetic joy (<s>muditā</s>), and equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>)? Here, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, in brief, cultivates the four immeasurables in three ways: with beings as object (<s>sattvālambana</s>), with <s>dharmas</s> as object (<s>dharmālambana</s>), and without object (<s>anālambana</s>). When the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, having established all beings in the three categories—those who are happy, those who are suffering, and those who are neither suffering nor happy—with the intention of providing happiness for those who desire happiness, pervades the ten directions with a mind of loving-kindness through the aspiration toward beings—this should be understood as his loving-kindness with beings as object. When one, perceiving only <s>dharmas</s>, seeing by way of convention the designating of beings upon mere <s>dharmas</s>, cultivates that very loving-kindness—this should be understood as his loving-kindness with <s>dharmas</s> as object. When one, not even conceptualizing <s>dharmas</s>, cultivates that very loving-kindness—this should be understood as his loving-kindness without object. Just as with loving-kindness having beings as object, <s>dharmas</s> as object, and without object, so compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity should also be understood. There, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, with regard to suffering beings, with the intention of removing suffering, cultivates a mind accompanied by compassion in the ten directions. This is his compassion. With regard to happy beings, with the intention of rejoicing in their happiness, one cultivates a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy in the ten directions. This is his sympathetic joy. With regard to those very three types of beings—those who are neither suffering nor happy, those who are suffering, and those who are happy—with the intention, respectively, of separation from the afflictions of delusion, aversion, and desire, one cultivates a mind accompanied by equanimity in the ten directions. This is his equanimity. There, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s immeasurables such as loving-kindness and the rest that have beings as object should be understood as shared with non-Buddhist <s>tīrthikas</s>. Those that have <s>dharmas</s> as object should be understood as shared with <s>Śrāvakas</s> and <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s> but not with <s>tīrthikas</s>. But the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s immeasurables that are without object should be understood as not shared with any <s>tīrthikas</s>, <s>Śrāvakas</s>, or <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s>. There, three of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s immeasurables should be understood as comprised in the intention of happiness: loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy. One immeasurable should be understood as comprised in the intention of benefit: namely, equanimity. And all these immeasurables of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> are called sympathy (<s>anukampā</s>). Therefore, <s>Bodhisattvas</s> endowed with them are called sympathetic.

body.text: tatra daśottaraśatākāraṃ duḥkhaṃ sattvadhātau saṃpaśyanto bodhisattvāḥ sattveṣu karuṇāṃ bhāvayanti / daśottaraśatākāraṃ duḥkhaṃ katamat / ekavidhaṃ duḥkham / aviśeṣeṇa pravṛttiduḥkhamārabhya sarvasattvāḥ pravṛttipatitā duḥkhitāḥ / dvividhaṃ duḥkham / chandamūlakaṃ yeṣāṃ [priyāṇāṃ] vastūnāṃ pariṇāmādanyathībhāvād duḥkhamutpadyate / sammohavipākañca duḥkhaṃ yaistīvraiḥ śārīrairveditaiḥ spṛṣṭastasminnātmabhāve ahamiti vā mameti vā sammūḍho 'tyarthaṃ śocati / yena dviśalyāṃ vedanāṃ vedayate kāyikīñcaitasikīñca / trividhaṃ duḥkhaṃ duḥkhaduḥkhatayā saṃskāraduḥkhatayā vipariṇāmaduḥkhatayā ca / caturvidhaṃ duḥkham / virahaduḥkhaṃ priyāṇāṃ visaṃyogādyadutpadyate / samucchedaduḥkhaṃ nikāyasabhāganikṣepānmaraṇādyadutpadyate / santatiduḥkhaṃ muttaratramṛtasya janmapāraṃparyeṇa yadutpadyate / atyantaduḥkhamaparinirvāṇadharmakāṇāṃ sattvānāṃ ye pañcopādānaskandhāḥ / pañcavidhaṃ duḥkham / kāmacchandaparyavasthāna pratyayaṃ vyāpādastyāna-middhauddhatya-kaukṛtya-vicikitsā-paryavasthānapratyayañca yaddūḥkham / ṣaḍvidhaṃ duḥkham / hetuduḥkhamāpayaheturniṣevaṇāt phaladuḥkhamapāyopapattitaḥ / bhogān punarārabhya paryeṣṭiduḥkhamārakṣāduḥkhamatṛptiduḥkhaṃ vipraṇāśaduḥkhañca / tadetadabhisamasya ṣaḍvidhaṃ duḥkhaṃ bhavati / saptavidhaṃ duḥkham / jātirduḥkhaṃ jarāvyādhirmaraṇamapriyasaṃyogaḥ priyavinābhāvaḥ yadapīcchanparyeṣamāṇo na labhate tadapi duḥkham / aṣṭavidhaṃ duḥkham / śītaduḥkhabhuṣṇaduḥkhaṃ jighatsāduḥkhaṃ pipasāduḥkhamasvātantryaduḥkham / ātmopakramaduḥkhaṃ tadyathā nigranthaprabhṛtīnām / paropakramaduḥkhaṃ tadyathā paṇiloṣṭasaṃsparśādibhiḥ parato daṃśamaśakādisaṃsparśaiśca /
body.translated_text: There, <s>Bodhisattvas</s>, perceiving one hundred and ten forms of suffering in the realm of beings, cultivate compassion toward beings. What are the one hundred and ten forms of suffering? One type of suffering: with regard to the suffering of continued existence (<s>pravṛttiduḥkha</s>) in general—all beings who have fallen into continued existence are suffering. Two types of suffering: suffering rooted in desire, which arises from the change and alteration of beloved things; and suffering that is the result of delusion, whereby one touched by intense bodily sensations (<s>vedanā</s>), confused about 'I' and 'mine' with regard to that bodily existence, grieves excessively—and thereby experiences a twofold painful feeling, physical and mental. Three types of suffering: the suffering of suffering (<s>duḥkhaduḥkhatā</s>), the suffering of conditioned existence (<s>saṃskāraduḥkhatā</s>), and the suffering of change (<s>vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā</s>). Four types of suffering: the suffering of separation, arising from the parting with the beloved; the suffering of extinction, arising from death, the falling away of one's class of existence; the suffering of continuity, arising from the succession of births of one who has died and been reborn; and the ultimate suffering—the five aggregates of clinging of beings who are not of the nature to attain <s>parinirvāṇa</s>. Five types of suffering: suffering conditioned by the hindrance of sensual desire, and suffering conditioned by the hindrances of ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt. Six types of suffering: suffering of cause, from engaging in the causes of misfortune; suffering of result, from birth in the realms of misfortune; and regarding possessions—the suffering of seeking, the suffering of guarding, the suffering of insatiability, and the suffering of loss. Seven types of suffering: birth is suffering, aging, illness, death, association with the disagreeable, separation from the beloved, and not obtaining what one desires and seeks—that too is suffering. Eight types of suffering: suffering of cold, suffering of heat, suffering of hunger, suffering of thirst, suffering of lack of freedom; suffering of self-inflicted harm, as with the <s>Nirgranthas</s> and others; suffering of harm inflicted by others, through contact with fists, clods, and the like, and through contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like from others;

body.text: īryāṃpathaikajātīyavihāraduḥkhañca / navavidhaṃ duḥkham / ātmavipattiduḥkhaṃ paravipattiduḥkhaṃ [jñātivipattiduḥkhaṃ bhogavipattiduḥkham] ārogyavipattiduḥkhaṃ śīlavipattiduḥkhaṃ dṛṣṭi-[vipattiduḥkhaṃ] dṛṣṭadhārmikaduḥkhaṃ sāmparāyikañca duḥkham / daśavidhaṃ duḥkham / bhojanakāyapariṣkāravaikalyaduḥkhaṃ pānayānavastrālaṅkārabhāṇḍopaṣkarapariṣkāravaikalyaduḥkhaṃ gandhamālyavilepanapariṣkāravaikalyaduḥkhaṃ nṛtyagītavāditrapariṣkāravaikalyaduḥkham ālokapariṣkāravaikalyaduḥkhaṃ strīpuruṣaparicaryākāyapariṣkāravaikalyaduḥkhañca daśamam punaranyaṃ navavidhaṃ duḥkhaṃ veditavyam / sarvaduḥkhaṃ mahāduḥkhaṃ sarvatomukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ vipratipattiduḥkhaṃ pravṛttiduḥkhamakāmakāraduḥkhaṃ vighātaduḥkhamānuṣaṅgikaṃ duḥkhaṃ sarvākārañca
body.translated_text: and the suffering of remaining in a single posture. Nine types of suffering: suffering from one's own misfortune, suffering from others' misfortune, suffering from the misfortune of relatives, suffering from the misfortune of possessions, suffering from the misfortune of health, suffering from the misfortune of moral conduct, suffering from the misfortune of [right] views, suffering in this life, and suffering in the next life. Ten types of suffering: suffering from lack of food and bodily requisites; suffering from lack of drink, vehicles, clothing, ornaments, vessels, utensils, and requisites; suffering from lack of perfumes, garlands, and ointments as requisites; suffering from lack of dancing, singing, and music as requisites; suffering from lack of light as a requisite; and the tenth, suffering from lack of requisites for the service and care of women and men. Furthermore, another ninefold suffering should be understood: all-suffering, great suffering, all-directional suffering, suffering of adversity, suffering of continued existence, suffering of involuntariness, suffering of obstruction, concomitant suffering, and all-aspected

body.text: duḥkham / tatra sarvaduḥkhaṃ yat pūrvahetusamutpannaṃ vartamānapratyayasamutpannañca / tatra mahāduḥkhaṃ yaddīrghaṃkālikaṃ pragāḍhaṃ citraṃ nirantarañca / tatra sarvatomukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ yannārakaṃ tairyagyonikaṃ pretalaukikaṃ sugatiparyāpannañca / tatra vipratipattiduḥkhaṃ yad dṛṣṭe vā dharme paravyatikramāt parāpakārakaraṇāllabhate samutthāpayati / viṣamabhojanaparibhogāddhātuvaiṣamyajaṃ duḥkhaṃ samutthāpayati / anayena vātmadṛṣṭadharmaduḥkhopakramāt svayaṃ kṛtaṃ duḥkhaṃ samutthāpayati / ayoniśomanaskāra-tadbahulavihāritayā vā kleśopakleśaparyavasthānaduḥkhaṃ pratyanubhavati / kāyavāṅmanoduścaritabāhalyādbā āyatyāmāpāyikaṃ duḥkhaṃ pratyanubhavati / tatra pravṛttiduḥkhaṃ yat ṣaḍākārādaniyamādutpadyate saṃsāre saṃsarataḥ / ātmabhāvāniyamādrājā bhūtvā āḍhyaḥ kṛpaṇo bhavati / mātāpitraniyamāt putradārāniyamāddāsīdāsakarmakarapauruṣeyāniyamāt
body.translated_text: suffering. There, 'all suffering' is that which is produced by prior causes and produced by present conditions. There, 'great suffering' is that which is long-lasting, deep, varied, and uninterrupted. There, 'all-encompassing suffering' is that which pertains to hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and those included in happy destinies. There, 'suffering from wrong conduct' is that which one obtains and produces in this very life through the transgression of others and through harming others; suffering born of the imbalance of bodily elements through the consumption of improper food; suffering self-produced through one's own improper approach to suffering in this present life; suffering of the envelopment of afflictions and secondary afflictions that one experiences through improper mental attention and abundant abiding therein; and suffering in the lower realms in the future that one experiences through the abundance of wrongdoing of body, speech, and mind. There, 'suffering of transmigration' is that which arises from the sixfold indeterminacy while wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s>: through the indeterminacy of personal existence, having been a king and wealthy, one becomes wretched; through the indeterminacy of parents, of sons and wives, of female and male servants and workers,

body.text: mitrāmātyajñātisālohitāniyamāt mātāpitarau bhūtvā yāvadvistareṇa mitrāmātyajñātisālohito bhūtvā 'pareṇa samayena saṃsarato vadhako bhavati pratyarthikaḥ pratyamitraḥ / bhogāniyamācca saṃsāre saṃsaran mahābhogo bhūtvā punarapareṇa samayena paramadaridro bhavati / tatrākāmakāraduḥkha yaddīrghāyuṣkāmasya akāmamalpāyuṣkatayotpadyate /
body.translated_text: through the indeterminacy of friends, ministers, relatives, and kinsmen—having been parents, and in detail having been friends, ministers, relatives, and kinsmen, at another time while transmigrating one becomes a murderer, an adversary, an enemy. And through the indeterminacy of possessions, while wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s>, having been one of great possessions, at another time one becomes utterly destitute. There, 'involuntary suffering' is that which arises involuntarily through being short-lived when one desires long life;

body.text: ābhirupyakāmasya cākāmaṃ vairupyataḥ / uccakulopapattikāmasya cākāmaṃ nīcakulopapattitaḥ / aiśvaryakāmasyākāmaṃ dāridryopanipātataḥ [mahā-]balakāmasya cākāmaṃ daurvalyopanipātata utpadyate / jñeyaṃ jñātukāmasya cākāmaṃ sammohājñānasamudācāra utpadyate / paraparājayakāmasya cākāmaṃ parāparājayādātmaparajayādyaddaḥkhamutpadyate / tatra vighātaduḥkhaṃ yadgṛhiṇāñca putradārādyapacayād yadutpadyate / pravrajitānāñca rāgādikleśopacayād yad duḥkhamutpadyate / yacca dukhaṃ durbhikṣopaghātādvā paracakropadhātādvā 'ṭavīdurgapraveśasambādha saṃkaṭopaghātādvā utpadyate / yacca duḥkhaṃ parāyattavṛttatayā utpadyate / yacca duḥkhaṃmaṅgapratyaṅgavaikalyopaghātād votpadyate / yacca duḥkhaṃ vadhabandhanacchedanatāḍanapravāsanādyupadyātādutpadyate / tatrānuṣaṅgikaṃ duḥkhaṃ yadaṣṭāsu lokadharmeṣu duḥkhaṃ naśana dharmake naṣṭe kṣayadharmake kṣīṇe jarādharmake jīrṇe vyādhidharmake vyādhite maraṇadharmake mṛte 'lābhato vā punarayaśasto vā nindāto vā yaddaḥkham / ityetadaṣṭavidhaṃ duḥkhaṃ prāryanāduḥkhañca / idamucyate ānuṣaṅgikaṃ duḥkham / tatra sarvākāraṃ duḥkhaṃ
body.translated_text: through ugliness when one desires beauty; through birth in a low family when one desires birth in a high family; through the onset of poverty when one desires sovereignty; through the onset of weakness when one desires great strength; through the arising of delusion and ignorance when one desires to know the knowable; through the suffering arising from being defeated by others and self-defeat when one desires to defeat others. There, 'suffering from ruin' is that which arises for householders from the loss of sons, wives, and the like; and that suffering which arises for renunciants from the increase of afflictions such as desire and the like; and that suffering which arises from the harm of famine, from the harm of hostile forces, or from the harm of entering the confines, difficulties, and narrow passes of wilderness; and that suffering which arises from being dependent on others for one's livelihood; and that suffering which arises from the harm of deformity or loss of limbs; and that suffering which arises from the afflictions of execution, imprisonment, cutting, beating, banishment, and the like. There, 'consequent suffering' (<s>ānuṣaṅgika duḥkha</s>) is that suffering in the eight worldly conditions (<s>lokadharmā</s>)—the suffering when what is subject to destruction is destroyed, what is subject to diminution is diminished, what is subject to aging has aged, what is subject to disease is diseased, what is subject to death has died; or the suffering from non-gain, from disrepute, or from blame. This eightfold suffering is that which is both noble and ignoble. This is called consequent suffering. There, 'all-aspect suffering'

body.text: yatpañcākāraṃ yathoddiṣṭasukhavipakṣeṇa duḥkhaṃ hetuduḥkhaṃ vedayitaduḥkhaṃ sukhābhāvamātraduḥkhaṃ veditayānupacchedaduḥkhaṃ naiṣkramyapravivekopaśamasaṃbodhisukhavipakṣeṇa vāgārikakāmadhātusaṃyogaja-vitarka-pṛthagjanaduḥkhaṃ pañcamaṃ veditavyam / ityetacca paścavidhaṃ duḥkham / aupakramikamupakaraṇavaikalyajaṃ dhātuvaiṣamyajaṃ priyavipariṇāmajaṃ traidhātukāvacarakleśapakṣyadoṣṭhulyaduḥkhañca pañcamam / ityetat pañcavidhaṃ pūrvakaṃ caikadhyamabhisaṃkṣipya daśavidhaṃ dukhaṃ sarvākāramityucyate /
body.translated_text: is that fivefold suffering opposed to the happiness as enumerated: causal suffering, experienced suffering, suffering that is the mere absence of happiness, suffering of the non-cessation of experience, and—the fifth—the suffering connected with the household life, the desire-realm, association, discursive thought, and the ordinary person, opposed to the happiness of renunciation, seclusion, pacification, and awakening. This fivefold suffering, together with the [further] five—suffering from harm, suffering born of lack of provisions, suffering born of the imbalance of elements, suffering born of the change of what is dear, and the fifth, suffering of heaviness (<s>dauṣṭhulya</s>) belonging to the side of the afflictions pervading the three realms—gathering the former and latter fivefold together, this tenfold suffering is called 'all-aspect suffering.'

body.text: iti pūrvakañca [pañcapañcāśadākāramidañca] pañcapañcāśadākāramaikadhyamabhisaṃkṣipya daśottaraśatākāraṃ duḥkhaṃ bhavati bodhisattvaḥ karuṇāyā ālambanaṃ yenālambanena bodhisattvānāṃ karuṇotpadyate vivardhate bhāvanāparipūriṃ gacchati /
body.translated_text: Thus, gathering together the former [fifty-five aspects] and this [fifty-five aspects] into one hundred and ten aspects of suffering—the <s>Bodhisattva</s> is the object of compassion through which the compassion of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> arises, increases, and reaches the fulfillment of cultivation.

body.text: ataśca mahato duḥkhaskandhādekānnaviṃśatiprakāraduḥkhālambanā mahākaruṇā pravartate / ekānnaviṃśatiprakāraṃ duḥkhaṃ katamat / sammohavipākaṃ duḥkhaṃ saṃskāraduḥkhatāsaṃgṛhītaṃ duḥkhamātyantikaṃ duḥkhaṃ hetuduḥkhaṃ jātiduḥkhaṃ svayaṃkṛtaupakramikaṃ duḥkhaṃ śīlavipattiduḥkhaṃ dṛṣṭivipattiduḥkhaṃ pūrvahetukaṃ duḥkhaṃ mahadduḥkhaṃ nārakaṃ duḥkhaṃ sugatisaṃgṛhītaṃ duḥkhaṃ sarvavipratipattijaṃ duḥkhaṃ sarvapravṛttiduḥkhamajñānaduḥkhamaupacayikaṃ duḥkhamānuṣaṅgikaṃ duḥkhaṃ vedayitaduḥkhaṃ dauṣṭhulyaduḥkhañceti /
body.translated_text: And from this great mass of suffering, great compassion (<s>mahākaruṇā</s>) operates with nineteen kinds of suffering as its object. What are the nineteen kinds of suffering? Suffering of the fruit of delusion, suffering comprised in the suffering of formations (<s>saṃskāraduḥkhatā</s>), ultimate suffering, causal suffering, suffering of birth, self-inflicted harmful suffering, suffering from the loss of moral conduct, suffering from the loss of right views, suffering with prior causes, great suffering, suffering of hell, suffering included in happy destinies, suffering from all wrong conduct, suffering of all transmigration, suffering of ignorance, suffering of accumulation, consequent suffering, experienced suffering, and suffering of heaviness (<s>dauṣṭhulya</s>).

body.text: tatra caturbhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ karuṇā mahākaruṇetyucyate gambhīraṃ sūkṣmaṃ durvijñeyaṃ sattvānāṃ duḥkhamālamvyotpannā bhavati / dīrghakālaparicitā ca bhavatyaneka kalpaśatasahasrābhyastā / tīvreṇa cābhogenālambane pravṛttā bhavati yadrūpeṇābhogenāyaṃ karuṇāviṣṭo bodhisattvaḥ sattvānāṃ duḥkhāpanayanahetoḥ svajīvitaśatānyapi parityajet prāgevaikaṃ jīvitaṃ prāgeva ca kāyapariṣkāram / sarvaduḥkhayātanāprakārāṃścodvahet / suviśuddhā ca bhavati tadyathā niṣṭhāgatānāśca bodhisattvānāṃ bodhisattvabhūmiviśuddhyā tathāgatānāñca tathāgatabhūmiviśuddhyā /
body.translated_text: There, compassion is called 'great compassion' for four reasons: it arises having taken as its object the suffering of beings that is profound, subtle, and difficult to understand. It has been long cultivated, practiced over many hundreds of thousands of <s>kalpas</s>. It operates with intense engagement toward its object—with such intensity of engagement that this <s>Bodhisattva</s>, pervaded by compassion, for the sake of removing the suffering of beings, would sacrifice even a hundred of his own lives—how much more so a single life, how much more mere bodily possessions! And he would endure all forms of suffering. And it is thoroughly purified—like that of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> who have reached the culmination, through the purification of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>-stages, and of <s>Tathāgatas</s>, through the purification of the <s>Tathāgata</s>-stage.

body.text: anena khalu daśottareṇākāraśatena ye bodhisattvaḥ karuṇāṃ bhāvayanti sattveṣu te sarvāṃ bodhisattvakaruṇāṃ bhāvayanti / te punaḥ kṣiprameva karuṇāśayaśuddhimadhigacchanti śuddhāśayabhūmipraviṣṭām / sattveṣu cātyarthaṃ snigdhacittāśca bhavanti premacittāśca kartukāmacittāścākhinnacittāśca duḥkhodbahanacittāśca karmaṇyavaśyacittāśca / na ca tathā duḥkhasatyamabhisamitavata āryaśrāvakasya niṣṭhāgatasya dūrībhūtā
body.translated_text: By this one hundred and ten aspects, <s>Bodhisattvas</s> who cultivate compassion toward beings cultivate all <s>Bodhisattva</s>-compassion. And they quickly attain the purification of the intention of compassion, which has entered the stage of pure superior intention. And toward beings they become extremely affectionate in mind, loving in mind, desirous of acting in mind, unwearied in mind, bearing-of-suffering in mind, and workable and pliant in mind. And the stream of consciousness accompanied by revulsion does not proceed in the manner of the noble <s>Śrāvaka</s> who has reached the culmination and has comprehended the truth of suffering, as it does for the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, who,

body.text: nirvit-sahagatā cittasaṃtatiḥ pravartate yathā bodhisattvasyura sattveṣu karuṇāpūrvaṅgamena cittena daśottarākāraśatapatitametaṃ mahāntaṃ duḥkhaskandhaṃ saṃpaśyataḥ / na ca bodhisattva evaṃ karuṇāparibhāvitamānasaḥ kiñcidādhyātmikabāhyaṃ vastu yanna parityajet / nāsti tacchīlasaṃvarasamādānaṃ yanna kuryāt / nāsti sa parāpakāraḥ kaścidyanna kṣamet / nāsti sa vīryārambho yannārabheta / nāsti taddhyānaṃ yanna samāpadyeta / nāsti sā prajñā yāṃ nānupraviśet / tasmāttathāgatāḥ pṛṣṭāḥ santaḥ-kutra pratiṣṭhitā bodhisattvasya bodhiriti-samyak vyākurvāṇā vyākurvanti karuṇāpratiṣṭhitā bodhisattvasya bodhiriti /
body.translated_text: with a mind preceded by compassion toward beings, perceives this great mass of suffering falling under the one hundred and ten aspects. The <s>Bodhisattva</s> whose mind is thus pervaded by compassion—there is nothing internal or external that he would not relinquish; there is no undertaking of moral discipline that he would not perform; there is no harm done by others that he would not endure; there is no exertion of vigor that he would not undertake; there is no <s>dhyāna</s> that he would not enter; there is no wisdom that he would not penetrate. Therefore, the <s>Tathāgatas</s>, when asked, 'On what is the awakening of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> established?'—answering correctly, declare: 'The awakening of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> is established on compassion.'

body.text: tatraikaikamatra yathānirdiṣṭamapramāṇa[mapramāṇayā] samṛddhyā samṛddhiṃ bodhisattvasya pravartate / apramāṇeṣṭhaphalaparigrāhakamapramāṇaiścākārairekāntakuśalairanavadyaiḥ pravartate / evamapramāṇabhāvanānuyuktasya bodhisattvasya catvāro 'nuśaṃsā veditavyāḥ / sāsyāpramāṇabhāvanā ādita eva paramadṛṣṭadharmasukhavihārāya bhavati / apramāṇapuṇyasaṃbhāraparigrahopacayāya bhavati / anuttarāyāṃ samyaksaṃbodhāvāśayadṛḍhatvāya bhavati / sattvānāṃ cārthe saṃsāre sarvaduḥkhodvahanāya bhavati /
body.translated_text: There, each one [of the immeasurables], as described, operates with immeasurable accomplishment for the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, and operates with immeasurable aspects that are exclusively wholesome and blameless, grasping immeasurable desired fruits. Thus, for the <s>Bodhisattva</s> who is devoted to the cultivation of the immeasurables, four benefits should be understood: That immeasurable cultivation serves, from the very beginning, as the supreme pleasant abiding in this present life. It serves for the acquisition and accumulation of an immeasurable store of merit. It serves for the firmness of intention toward the unsurpassed, perfect awakening. And it serves for enduring all suffering in <s>saṃsāra</s> for the welfare of beings.

body.text: iti bodhisattvabhūmāvādhāre yogasthāne ṣoḍaśamaṃ pūjāsevāpramāṇapaṭalam /
body.translated_text: Thus, in the <s>Bodhisattvabhūmi</s>, in the Foundation Section of Yoga, the sixteenth chapter, the <s>Pūjāsevāpramāṇa-paṭala</s> (Chapter on Worship, Service, and the Immeasurables), [is completed].

body.text: uddānam /
body.translated_text: Summary verse (<s>uddāna</s>):

children.translated_text: Moral shame, fortitude, and unweariness, knowledge of treatises and the world likewise,
the correct reliances, and the analytical knowledges,
the accumulations and the factors of awakening, calm abiding and insight,
skill in means, <s>dhāraṇī</s>, and aspirational vows,
the three concentrations should be known, and the fourfold summary of the <s>Dharma</s>. //

body.text: tatra katamad bodhisattvānāṃ hrīvyapatrāpyam / tat samāsato dvividhaṃ veditavyam / svabhāvataścādhiṣṭhānataśca /
body.translated_text: There, what is the moral shame and moral dread (<s>hrīvyapatrāpya</s>) of <s>Bodhisattvas</s>? It should be understood in brief as twofold: by essential nature and by basis.

body.text: avadyasamudācāre ātmana evāpratirūpatāṃ viditvā bodhisattvasya lajjā hrīḥ / tatraiva pareṣāṃ bhayagauravāllajjā vyapatrāpyam / sā punarllajjā bodhisattvasya prakṛtyaiva tīvrā bhavati prāgevābhyastā / evaṃ svabhāvato bodhisattvasya hrīvyapatrābhyaṃ veditavyam /
body.translated_text: Knowing the unfittingness for oneself of blameworthy conduct, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s embarrassment is moral shame (<s>hrī</s>). In that very [blameworthy conduct], embarrassment out of fear and respect for others is moral dread (<s>vyapatrāpya</s>). That embarrassment, moreover, is by nature intense in the <s>Bodhisattva</s>—how much more so when cultivated! Thus, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s moral shame and dread should be understood by essential nature.

body.text: adhiṣṭhānaṃ punaḥ samāsataścaturvidham / bodhisattvakaraṇīyasyānanuṣṭhāne yā lajjā / idaṃ prathamamadhiṣṭhānam / tathā bodhisattvākaraṇīyasyānuṣṭhāne yā lajjā / idaṃ dvitīyamadhiṣṭhānam / tathā bodhisattvasyātmanaḥ praticchannapāpatāyāṃ yā lajjā / idaṃ tṛtīyamadhiṣṭhānam / tathā bodhisattvasya kaukṛtye samutpanne sapratisaraṇe ānuṣaṅgike yā lajjā / idaṃ caturthamadhiṣṭhānam / evamadhiṣṭhānato veditavyam /
body.translated_text: The basis, moreover, is in brief fourfold. The embarrassment at the non-performance of what is a <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s duty—this is the first basis. Likewise, the embarrassment at the performance of what is not a <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s duty—this is the second basis. Likewise, the embarrassment of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> at concealing his own faults—this is the third basis. Likewise, the embarrassment of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> when remorse has arisen, which has a remedy and is consequent—this is the fourth basis. Thus it should be understood by basis.

body.text: tatra katamā bodhisattvasya dhṛtibalādhānatā / sāpi dvividhā draṣṭavyā / svabhāvataścādhiṣṭhānataśca /
body.translated_text: There, what is the fortitude and strength of resolve (<s>dhṛtibalādhānatā</s>) of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>? That too should be seen as twofold: by essential nature and by basis.

body.text: kliṣṭacittasanniyacchanatā kleśavaśā[na]nuyāyitā duḥkhādhivāsanaśīlatā vicitraprabhūtodriktairapi bhayabhairavairāmukhaiḥ samyak prayogāvikampanatā prakṛtisattvayogāt pratisaṃkhyānādvā dhīratā / itīyaṃ dhṛtibalādhānatā svabhāvato veditavyā /
body.translated_text: The restraining of a defiled mind, the non-following of the power of defilements, the disposition to endure suffering, the non-wavering from correct practice even when confronted by various, abundant, and intense fears and terrors—the courage that comes from the natural strength of character or from reflection. This should be understood as fortitude and strength of resolve by essential nature.

body.text: asyāḥ khalu bodhisattvānāṃ dhṛtibalādhānatāyāḥ samāsataḥ pañcavidhamadhiṣṭhānaṃ veditavyam / vicitraḥ saṃsāraduḥkhopanipāto vicitrā vineyakṛtā vipratipattiḥ / dīrghakālikaḥ sattvānāmarthe saṃsārābhyupagamaḥ / paravādibhirākalanānuyogo mahatyāñca pariṣadi dharmadeśanā / sarvabodhi [sattva-]śikṣā[padā]bhyupagamaḥ / udāragaṃbhīradharmaśravaṇañca pañcamamadhiṣṭhānaṃ veditavyam /
body.translated_text: The basis of this fortitude and strength of resolve of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> should be understood in brief as fivefold: the various onslaughts of suffering in <s>saṃsāra</s>; the various wrong conduct committed by those to be trained; the long-term acceptance of <s>saṃsāra</s> for the welfare of beings; the persistence of challenges from rival doctrinaires and the teaching of the <s>Dharma</s> in a great assembly; the undertaking of all the <s>Bodhisattva</s>-training-rules; and the hearing of lofty and profound <s>dharmas</s>—this should be understood as the fifth basis.

body.text: tatra pañcabhiḥ kāraṇairaparikhinnamānasatā bodhisattvānāṃ sarvasamyak prayogeṣu veditavyā / iha bodhisattvaḥ prakṛtyā balavān bhavati yena na parikhidyate / punaḥ saivākhinnamānasatā 'nena punaḥ punarabhyastā bhavati yena na parikhidyate / punarupāyaparigṛhītenavīryāṃrambheṇa prayukto bhavati yena paurvāparyeṇa viśeṣaṃ samanupaśyan na parikhidyate / tīvreṇa ca prajñāpratisaṃkhyānabalena samanvāgato bhavati yena na parikhidyate / tīvrañcāsya bodhisattvasya sattveṣu kāruṇyacittamanukampācittaṃ satatasamitaṃ pratyupasthitaṃ bhavati yena na parikhidyate /
body.translated_text: There, the unwearied mind (<s>aparikhinnamānasatā</s>) of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> in all correct practices should be understood through five causes. Here, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> is by nature strong, by which he is not wearied. Again, that very unwearied mind has been repeatedly cultivated by him, by which he is not wearied. Again, he is engaged in vigor that is accompanied by skillful means, by which, seeing progressive distinction in sequence, he is not wearied. He is endowed with the intense power of wisdom and discernment, by which he is not wearied. And the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s intense mind of compassion and sympathetic concern toward beings is constantly present, by which he is not wearied.

body.text: tatra katamā bodhisattvasya śāstrajñayā / iha bodhisattvena pañcavidhāsthānānyārabhya nāmakāya-padakāya-vyañjanakāya-pratisaṃyukto dharmaḥ parataḥ sugṛhīto bhavati / vacasā ca suparicitaḥ / tasyaiva ca dharmasyārthaḥ parato vā suśruto bhavati / svayaṃ vā suvici[nti]to bhavati svabhyūhitaḥ / evamapi ca dharmajñenārthajñena bodhisattvena tasyaiva ca dharmasyārthasyāvismaraṇāya prayogo 'nirākṛto bhavatyanyasya cābhinavasyābhinavasyottarottarasya dharmārthaviśeṣasya jñānāya / śrutacintāniṣṭhāgatenāpi cānena kālāntarakṛtaḥ paripākaḥ prasādaḥ tasmindharme cārthe ca pratilabdho bhavati / ebhirākārairbodhisattvasyāpramāṇā paripūrṇā aviparītā ca śāstrajñatā veditavyā /
body.translated_text: There, what is the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s knowledge of treatises (<s>śāstrajñatā</s>)? Here, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, beginning with the five fields [of knowledge], has well-grasped from others the <s>Dharma</s> that is connected with word-groups (<s>nāmakāya</s>), sentence-groups (<s>padakāya</s>), and syllable-groups (<s>vyañjanakāya</s>). He has also well-familiarized [it] through recitation. And the meaning of that very <s>Dharma</s> has been either well-heard from others, or well-reflected upon and well-reasoned by himself. And even for this <s>Bodhisattva</s> who is a knower of both the <s>Dharma</s> and its meaning, the effort for not forgetting that very <s>Dharma</s> and its meaning is unrejected, as is [the effort] for knowing ever newer and higher distinctions of <s>Dharma</s> and meaning. And even for this one who has reached the culmination of hearing and reflection, there is, over time, a matured confidence—a faith—obtained in that <s>Dharma</s> and its meaning. Through these aspects, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s knowledge of treatises should be understood as immeasurable, complete, and unerring.

body.text: tatra katamā bodhisattvasya lokajñatā / iha bodhisattvaḥ sattvalokamārabhyaivaṃ yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti-kṛcchraṃ vatāyaṃ loka āpanno yaduta jāyate 'pi jīryate 'pi mriyate 'pi cyavatepyupapadyatepyatha ca punaramī sattvā jarāmaraṇasyottari niḥsaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ [na] prajānantīti / punaḥ sattvalokasyaiva kaṣāyotsadakālatāñca yathābhūtaṃ
body.translated_text: There, what is the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s knowledge of the world (<s>lokajñatā</s>)? Here, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, regarding the world of beings (<s>sattvaloka</s>), knows truly thus: 'Alas, this world has fallen into misery—namely, it is born, it ages, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn. And yet these beings do not truly know the escape beyond old age and death.' Furthermore, he truly knows the periods of ascendancy of the defilements in the world of beings

body.text: prajānāti / niṣkaṣāyānutsadakaṣāyakālatāñca yaduta pañcakaṣāyānārabhya āyuṣkaṣāyaṃ [sattvakaṣāyaṃ] kleśakaṣāyaṃ kalpakaṣāyam / tadyathā etarhyalpaṃ jīvitaṃ manuṣyāṇāṃ yaściraṃ jīvati sa varṣaśatam / tadyathaitarhi sattvā yadbhūyasā [a]mātṛjñā apitṛjñā aśrāmaṇyā abrāhmaṇyā na kulajyeṣṭhāpacāyakā nārthakarā na kṛtyakarā na iha loke na paraloke avadye bhayadarśino na dānāni dadati na puṇyāni kurvanti nopavāsamupavasanti na śīlaṃ samādāya vartante / tadyathaitarhi yadbhūyasā 'dharmarāgāśca viṣamalobhāśca śastrādānadaṇḍādānakalahabhaṇḍanavigrahavivādaśāṭhyavañcananikṛtimṛṣāvādamithyādharmasaṃgṛhītā anekavidhāḥ pāpakā akuśalā dharmāḥ prajñāyante / tadyathaitarhi saddharmapralopāya saddharmāntardhānāya saddharmapratirūpakāṇi prabhūtāni prādurbhūtāni mithyādharmārtha-santīraṇāpūrvikāṇi / tadyathā etarhi durbhikṣāntarakalpasamāsannāni pracurāṇi durbhikṣāṇyupalabhyante / rogāntarakalpasamāsannāśca rogāśca pracurā upalabhyante /
body.translated_text: and the periods free from defilement and periods of mild defilement—namely, regarding the five defilements (<s>kaṣāya</s>): the defilement of lifespan (<s>āyuṣkaṣāya</s>), [the defilement of beings (<s>sattvakaṣāya</s>),] the defilement of afflictions (<s>kleśakaṣāya</s>), and the defilement of the age (<s>kalpakaṣāya</s>). For instance, at present the lifespan of humans is short—one who lives long lives a hundred years. For instance, at present beings for the most part do not acknowledge their mothers, do not acknowledge their fathers, are disrespectful to ascetics and brahmins, do not honor family elders, do not act for [others'] benefit, do not perform [their] duties, do not see danger in wrongdoing either in this world or the next, do not give gifts, do not perform meritorious deeds, do not observe the fast-days, and do not undertake moral conduct. For instance, at present for the most part there manifests immorality-desire, crooked greed, and manifold evil, unwholesome <s>dharmas</s> embraced by wrong conduct—taking up weapons, taking up punishments, quarrels, disputes, conflicts, contentions, deceit, fraud, treachery, and false speech. For instance, at present, for the destruction and disappearance of the true <s>Dharma</s>, many counterfeits of the true <s>Dharma</s> have appeared, preceded by the wrong determination of <s>Dharma</s> and its meaning. For instance, at present, close to the intermediate age of famine, many famines are found. Close to the intermediate age of disease, many diseases are found.

body.text: śastrāntarakalpasamāsannāśca pracurāḥ śastrakāḥ prāṇātipātā upalabhyante / na tu tathā pūrvamāsīt / evaṃ hi bodhisattvaḥ sattvalokamārabhya lokajño bhavati / punarbodhisattvo bhājanalokasya saṃvartavivartaṃ yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti yathā bhājanalokaḥ saṃvartate vivartate ca / punarbodhisattvo lokañca [loka]samudayañca lokanirodhañca lokasamudayagāminīñca pratipadaṃ lokanirodhagāminīñca pratipadaṃ lokasyāsvādamādīnavañca niḥsaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti / punarbodhisattvaḥ cakṣuryāvanmanaḥ arūpiṇaśca skandhāṃścāturmahābhautikañca puruṣasya samucchrayametāvanmanuṣyatvamityucyate / tatra yā saṃjñā ātmā vā sattvo veti saṃjñāmātramevaitat / tatra yā pratijñā ahaṃ cakṣuṣā rūpāṇi paśyāmi yāvanmanasā dharmāna vijānāmīti pratijñāmātrameva tat / tatra yo vyavahāra ityapi sa āyuṣmānevaṃnāmā evaṃjātīya evaṃgotra evamāhāra evaṃ sukhaduḥkhapratisaṃvedī evaṃ dīryāyurevaṃ cirasthitika evamāyuṣparyanta iti vyavahāramātramevaitaditi sarvaṃ yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti / iti hi sa bodhisattvaḥ sattvalokapravṛttiñca bhājanalokapravṛttiñca aṣṭākāralokopaparīkṣārthañca [lokaparamārthaṃ ca] yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti / tasmāllokajñaityucyate / punarbodhisattvo vṛddhatarakaṃ guṇaprativiśiṣṭatarakaṃ dṛṣṭvā samyak saṃbhāṣayatyutthāyāsanenopanimantrayati
body.translated_text: Close to the intermediate age of weapons, many acts of killing with weapons are found. This was not so formerly. Thus the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, regarding the world of beings, is a knower of the world. Furthermore, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> truly knows the formation and dissolution of the physical world (<s>bhājanaloka</s>)—how the physical world forms and dissolves. Furthermore, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> truly knows the world and the origin of the world, the cessation of the world and the path leading to the origin of the world and the path leading to the cessation of the world, and the gratification, danger, and escape of the world. Furthermore, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> [knows]: the eye up to the mind, the formless aggregates (<s>skandhas</s>), and the bodily frame constituted of the four great elements—this much is called 'being human.' Therein, whatever conception [there is of] a self or a being is merely a conception. Therein, whatever assertion 'I see forms with the eye' up to 'I cognize <s>dharmas</s> with the mind' is merely an assertion. Therein, whatever convention—'This venerable one is of such-and-such name, of such-and-such birth, of such-and-such lineage, of such-and-such nourishment, experiencing such-and-such happiness and suffering, of such-and-such lifespan, of such-and-such long duration, of such-and-such extent of life'—is merely a convention. All this he truly knows. Thus the <s>Bodhisattva</s> truly knows the course of the world of beings, the course of the physical world, the eightfold examination of the world, [and the ultimate nature of the world]. Therefore he is called 'a knower of the world.' Furthermore, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, upon seeing one who is older and of superior qualities, properly greets [him], rises and offers a seat,

body.text:
abhivādanavandanapratyutthānāñjalisāmīcīkarma pravartayati / tulyaṃ vā punarvayasā guṇaiśca dṛṣṭvā samyagālapati pratisamodayati ślakṣṇairmadhurairvacanapathaiḥ / na cānena saha mānamāśrityātmāna paritulayati / hīnaṃ vā punarvayasā guṇaiśca dṛṣṭvā śaktyā guṇādhānamārabhya protsāhayati / bhūtañcāsya guṇaṃ svalpamapyudbhāvayati / bhūtañca doṣaṃ praticchādayati / na vivṛṇoti yenāsya syānmaṃkubhāvaḥ / na cainamavamanyate / nāpyarthikaṃ kenaciddharmāmiṣeṇa taṃ jñātvā vimukho bhavati bhṛkuṭīkṛtaḥ / nāpi cainaṃ skhalite 'vahasati / nāpi vinipatitaṃ paribhavati / tathā sarveṣāmeva hīnatulyaviśiṣṭānāṃ sattvānāṃ pūrvābhibhāṣī ca bhavati / ehi svāgatavādī samyak pratiśāmakaśca samyagdharmāmiṣābhyāṃ yathāśaktyā saṃgrāhakaśca / nāpi ca sattveṣu kuṭilagāmbhīryopeto bhavati na garvitaḥ kenacidevocchrayaviśeṣeṇa / yathopāttaṃ sattvaṃ sarvopakaraṇairapi nādhyupekṣate glānaṃ vā svasthaṃ vā ānulomikena ca kāyavākkarmaṇā / yathā saṃstutaṃ tathaivāsaṃstutaṃ sarvaṃ mitrasakhā ca bhavati vigatapratyarthikaḥ / sarveṣāñcānāthānāmapratisaraṇānāṃ sattvānāṃ yathāśaktyā yathābalaṃ cārthakriyāṃ karoti / na ca kenacit paryāyeṇa pareṣāṃ duḥkhadaurmanasyamupasaṃharati kaccideṣāṃ muhūrtamapyasparśavihāro bhavatviti / etameva pratyayaṃ kṛtvā parihasannapi paraiḥ saha yuktaparihāso bhavati nāyuktaparihāsaḥ /
asatyavacanāni ca na kathayatyapi niratyayaiḥ paramaviśrambhopagatairvayasyakaiḥ / na ca ciraṃ pareṣāṃ krudhyati / kroddho 'pi ca pareṣāṃ na marmāṇi kīrtayati / paraiśca kāyena vācā vāhataḥ san pratisaṃkhyāya dharmatāṃ vā pratisarati ātmānameva vā 'parādhikaṃ paśyati / sthiracittaśca bhavatyacalaḥ / sthirakāyavāṅmanaḥpracāraścaturdaśamalakarmāpagataśca bhavati / ṣaḍdigbhāgapraticchannaḥ catuḥpāpamitraparivarjitaḥ / catuḥkalyāṇamitraparigṛhītaḥ / etacca yathāsūtrameva sarvaṃ veditavyam / dṛṣṭadharmahitārthaṃ vā bhogapratisaṃyuktamārabhya utthānasaṃpanno bhavatyārakṣāsaṃpannaḥ samajīvī / ca laukikeṣu ca śilpakarmasthāneṣu kauśalyaprāptaḥ / aśaṭhaśca bhavatyamāyāvī na paravañcanaśīlaḥ / hrīmāṃśca bhavatyavadyasamudācāriṣu / cāritrasampannaśca
body.translated_text: performs salutation, homage, rising, hands-joined reverence, and acts of respectful conduct. And upon seeing one equal in age and qualities, he properly engages in conversation, responds kindly with gentle and sweet speech. He does not compare himself with the other out of conceit. And upon seeing one younger in age and qualities, he encourages him to strive according to his ability, beginning with the acquisition of virtues. He highlights even a small genuine virtue [of that person]. And he conceals genuine faults, not exposing them in a way that would cause embarrassment. He does not despise him. Nor, knowing someone to be in need of something—whether <s>Dharma</s> or material—does he turn away with a frown. Nor does he laugh at one who has stumbled. Nor does he disparage one who has fallen. Likewise, toward all beings—inferior, equal, and superior—he speaks first, saying 'Come, welcome!' and properly calming [them], properly gathering [them] with both <s>Dharma</s> and material gifts according to his ability. He is not crooked or deceptive toward beings, nor is he proud on account of any particular distinction. He does not neglect a being once taken under his care, whether ill or well, [attending to them] with all provisions and with harmonious bodily and verbal conduct. Just as toward an acquaintance, so toward a stranger—toward all he is a friend and companion, free from enmity. And for all beings who are without protector and without refuge, he acts for their welfare according to his ability and power. And by no means does he bring suffering and distress to others, [thinking:] 'May they not have even a moment's contact with pleasant abiding.' Making this very consideration, even when joking with others, he jokes appropriately, not inappropriately. And he does not speak false words even among the most intimate, supremely trusted companions with whom there is no offense. He does not remain angry at others for long. Even when angry, he does not proclaim the vulnerable points of others. And when struck by others in body or speech, having reflected, he either takes recourse to the nature of things or sees himself alone as being at fault. He is steady-minded and unshakable. He is of steady conduct in body, speech, and mind, free from the fourteen impure actions. He is guarded in the six directions, free from the four bad friends, and embraced by the four good friends. All of this should be understood exactly as stated in the <s>sūtras</s>. For the purpose of benefit and welfare in the present life, beginning with the acquisition of possessions, he is endowed with industry, endowed with protection, of balanced livelihood. He is skilled in worldly arts and crafts. He is without deceit, without guile, and not disposed to cheating others. He is possessed of moral shame regarding blameworthy conduct. He is endowed with proper conduct

body.text: bhavati tadgurūkaścāritrarakṣakaḥ / nikṣiptasya viśvāsena paradraviṇasya na drogdhā bhavati / upāttasya parata ṛṇasya na visaṃvādayitā bhavati / dāyādasya ca na parivañcayitā bhavati / ratnaṃ vā ratnasammatamupādāya yāvat kārṣāpaṇe 'pi sammūḍhānāṃ na vipralambhayitā bhavati vipralobhyainām / tathā laukikīṣu vyavahāranītiṣu laukānugrahakāriṣu paṭurbhavati / teṣu ca teṣvarthakaraṇīyeṣu parairāyācitaḥ san sahāyībhāvaṃ gacchati na vikampate nānyenānyaṃ pratisarati / susaṃprayukta-karmāntaśca bhavati na kuprayukta-karmāntaḥ / rājyaṃ vā punaḥ kārayan dharmeṇa kārayati nāgharmeṇa / na ca daṇḍarucirbhavati / dauḥśīlyācca mahājanakāyaṃ vyāvartayitvā śīlesu samādāpayati / tathāryairaṣṭābhirvyavahāraiḥ samanvāgato bhavati / dṛṣṭe dṛṣṭavāditayā śrute mate vijñāte vijñātavāditayā adṛṣṭe 'dṛṣṭavāditayā aśrute 'mate 'vijñāte avijñātavāditayā ityebhirevaṃ bhāgīyairdharmaiḥ samanvāgato bodhisattvo yathā loke vijñātavyo yathā loke vartitavyaṃ tatsarvaṃ yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti tasmāllokajña ityucyate /
body.translated_text: and values conduct, guarding it. He does not betray goods entrusted to him in confidence. He does not default on debts incurred from others. He does not cheat heirs. He does not deceive or defraud the confused regarding anything from a gem or valued jewel down to even a <s>kārṣāpaṇa</s> (coin). Likewise, he is skilled in worldly customs of conduct that benefit people. And when requested by others to assist in their various tasks, he becomes a companion—he does not waver or defer to another. He is well-organized in his undertakings, not poorly organized. If governing a kingdom, he governs according to <s>Dharma</s>, not contrary to <s>Dharma</s>. He is not fond of punishment. He turns the great multitude away from immorality and establishes them in moral conduct. Likewise, he is endowed with the eight noble modes of expression: saying one has seen what one has seen, saying one has cognized what one has cognized, saying one has not seen what one has not seen, and saying one has not cognized what one has not cognized. Endowed with such <s>dharmas</s>, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> truly knows all that is to be known in the world and how one is to conduct oneself in the world. Therefore he is called 'a knower of the world.'

body.text: tatra kathaṃ bodhisattvaścaturṣu pratisaraṇeṣu prayujyate / iha bodhisattvaḥ arthārthī parato dharmaṃ śruṇoti na vyañjanābhisaṃskārārthī / so 'rthārthī dharmaṃ śuṇvan na vyañjanārthī prākṛtayāpi vācā dharmaṃ deśayamānamarthapratisaraṇo bodhisattvaḥ satkṛtya śṛṇoti / punarbodhisattvaḥ kālāpadeśañca [mahāpadeśañca] yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti / prajānan yuktipratiśaraṇo bhavati na sthavireṇābhijñātena vā pudgalena tathāgatena vā [saṃghena vā] ime dharmā bhāṣitā iti pudgalapratisaraṇo bhavati / sa evaṃ yuktipratisaraṇo na pudgalapratisaraṇastattvārthāt na vicalati / a-parapratyayaśca bhavati dharmeṣu punarbodhisattvastathāgate viviṣṭaśraddho niviṣṭaprasāda ekāntiko vacasyabhiprasannastathāgata-nītārthaṃ sūtraṃ pratisarati na neyārtham / nītārthaṃ sūtraṃ pratisaran asaṃhāryo bhavatyasmāddharmavinayāt / tathāhi neyārthasya sūtrasya nānāmukhaprakṛtārthavibhāgo 'niścitaḥ saṃdehakaro bhavati / sacetpunarbodhisattvo nītārthe 'pi sūtre 'naikāntikaḥ syādevamasau saṃhāryaḥ syādasmāddharmavinayāt / punarbodhisattvo 'dhigamajñāne sāradarśī bhavati na śrutacintādharmārthavijñānamātrake / sa yadbhāvanāmayena jñānena jñātavyaṃ na tacchakyaṃ śrutacintāvijñānamātrakeṇa vijñātumiti
body.translated_text: There, how does the <s>Bodhisattva</s> apply himself to the four reliances (<s>pratisaraṇa</s>)? Here, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> listens to the <s>Dharma</s> from others seeking the meaning, not seeking the embellishment of words. Listening to the <s>Dharma</s> seeking the meaning and not the words, even when someone teaches the <s>Dharma</s> in common speech, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, relying on the meaning, listens respectfully. Furthermore, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> truly knows the proper occasion [of teaching] [and the great authorities]. Knowing [them], he becomes one who relies on reasoning (<s>yukti</s>), not one who relies on the person—[thinking:] 'These <s>dharmas</s> were spoken by an elder, a renowned person, the <s>Tathāgata</s>, [or the <s>Saṃgha</s>].' Thus relying on reasoning and not on the person, he does not deviate from the true meaning. And he becomes one who is independent of others in <s>dharmas</s>. Furthermore, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, having distinguished faith and settled confidence in the <s>Tathāgata</s>, being absolutely devoted to his word, relies on the <s>sūtras</s> of definitive meaning (<s>nītārtha</s>) taught by the <s>Tathāgata</s>, not on those of provisional meaning (<s>neyārtha</s>). Relying on <s>sūtras</s> of definitive meaning, he becomes unshakable from this <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s>. For indeed, the meaning-analysis of a <s>sūtra</s> of provisional meaning, being of manifold nature, is uncertain and causes doubt. But if the <s>Bodhisattva</s> were not definitive even regarding <s>sūtras</s> of definitive meaning, then he could be shaken from this <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s>. Furthermore, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> sees the essence in the knowledge of realization (<s>adhigamajñāna</s>), not in mere knowledge through hearing and reflection of <s>Dharma</s> and its meaning. Knowing that what is to be known through wisdom born of meditation (<s>bhāvanāmaya jñāna</s>) cannot be known through mere knowledge of hearing and reflection,

body.text: viditvā paramagambhīrānapi tathāgatabhāṣitāndharmān śrutvā na pratikṣipati nāpavadati / evaṃ hi bodhisattvaścaturṣupratisaraṇeṣu prayujyate / evañca punaḥ suprayukto bhavati / tatraiṣu caturṣu pratisaraṇeṣu samāsataścaturṇāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ saṃprakāśitam / bhāṣitasyārthasya yukteḥ śāstuḥ bhāvanāmayasya cādhigamajñānasya / sarvaiśca [punaśca]turbhiḥ pratisaraṇaiḥ samyakprayogasamārambhagatasya bodhisattvasyāvibhrāntaniryāṇamabhidyotitaṃ bhavati /
body.translated_text: having heard even supremely profound <s>dharmas</s> spoken by the <s>Tathāgata</s>, he does not reject or disparage [them]. Thus the <s>Bodhisattva</s> applies himself to the four reliances. And thus he becomes well-applied. There, in brief, in these four reliances, the authority of four [things] has been elucidated: of the meaning of what is spoken, of reasoning, of the Teacher, and of the realization-knowledge born of meditation. And through all four reliances, the unerring progress of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> who has entered upon right practice has been illuminated.

body.text: tatra katamā bodhisattvasya catasro bodhisattvapratisaṃvidaḥ / yatsarvadharmāṇāṃ sarvaparyāyeṣu yāvadbhāvikatayā yathāvadbhāvikatayā ca bhāvanāmayamasaktamavivartyaṃ jñānam / iyameṣāṃ dharmapratisaṃvit / yatpunaḥ sarvadharmāṇāmeva sarvalakṣaṇeṣu yāvadbhāvikatayā yathāvadbhāvikatayā ca bhāvanāmayamasaktamavivartyaṃ jñānam / iyameṣāmarthapratisaṃvit / yatpunaḥ sarvadharmāṇāmeva sarvanirvacaneṣu yāvadbhāvikatayā yathāvadbhāvikatayā ca bhāvanāmayamasaktamavivartyaṃ jñānam / iyameṣāṃ niruktipratisaṃvit / yatpunaḥ sarvadharmāṇāmeva sarvaprakārapadaprabhedeṣu yāvadbhāvikatayā yathāvadbhāvikatayā ca bhāvanāmayamasaktamavivartyaṃ jñānam / iyameṣāṃ pratibhānapratisaṃvat / etāścatasro bodhisattvapratisaṃvido niśrityo 'prameyaṃ bodhisattvānāṃ pañcasthānakauśalyaṃ veditavyam / skandhakauśalyaṃ dhātvāyatanapratītyasamutpādasthānāsthānakauśalyañca / ebhiścaturbhirākāraiḥ / sarvadharmā bodhisattvena svayañca svabhisaṃbuddhā bhavanti / pareṣāñca suprakāśitāḥ / ata uttari svayamabhisaṃbodho nāsti kutaḥ punaḥ pareṣāṃ prakāśanā /
body.translated_text: What therein are the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s four analytical knowledges (<s>pratisaṃvid</s>)? That unattached, irreversible knowledge born of cultivation, regarding the extent and manner of all <s>dharmas</s> in all their synonymous expressions—this is the analytical knowledge of <s>dharmas</s> (<s>dharmapratisaṃvid</s>). That unattached, irreversible knowledge born of cultivation, regarding the extent and manner of all <s>dharmas</s> in all their characteristics—this is the analytical knowledge of meaning (<s>arthapratisaṃvid</s>). That unattached, irreversible knowledge born of cultivation, regarding the extent and manner of all <s>dharmas</s> in all their etymologies—this is the analytical knowledge of language (<s>niruktipratisaṃvid</s>). That unattached, irreversible knowledge born of cultivation, regarding the extent and manner of all <s>dharmas</s> in all their varied expressions and classifications—this is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (<s>pratibhānapratisaṃvid</s>). Relying on these four analytical knowledges of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, the immeasurable skill of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> in five subjects is to be understood: skill in the aggregates (<s>skandha</s>), elements (<s>dhātu</s>), sense-bases (<s>āyatana</s>), dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>), and the possible and impossible (<s>sthānāsthāna</s>). Through these four modes, all <s>dharmas</s> are both self-realized by the <s>Bodhisattva</s> and well-illuminated for others. Beyond this there is no self-realization; how much less is there any further illumination for others.

body.text: tatra katamo bodhisattvasya bodhisaṃbhāraḥ / sa dvividho draṣṭavyaḥ / puṇyasaṃbhāro jñānasaṃbhāraśca / tasya punardvividhasyāpi saṃbhārasya vistaravibhāgo veditavyaḥ / tadyathā svaparārthapaṭale / sa punaḥ puṇyajñānasaṃbhāro bodhisattvasya prathame kalpāsaṃkhyeye mṛdurveditavyo dvitīye madhyastṛtīye 'dhimātro veditavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: What therein is the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s accumulation for awakening (<s>bodhisaṃbhāra</s>)? It is to be seen as twofold: the accumulation of merit (<s>puṇyasaṃbhāra</s>) and the accumulation of knowledge (<s>jñānasaṃbhāra</s>). The detailed classification of both types of accumulation is to be understood as in the Chapter on One's Own and Others' Welfare. Furthermore, that accumulation of merit and knowledge of the <s>Bodhisattva</s> is to be understood as mild in the first incalculable <s>kalpa</s> (eon), moderate in the second, and intense in the third.

body.text: kathaṃ bodhisattvaḥ saptatriṃsatsu bodhipakṣyeṣu dharmeṣu yogaṃ karoti / iha bodhisattvaścatasro bodhisattvapratisaṃvido niśrityopāya-parigṛhītena jñānena saptatriṃśadbodhipakṣyāndharmānyathābhūtaṃ prajānāti / na caitān sākṣātkaroti / sa
body.translated_text: How does the <s>Bodhisattva</s> practice the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (<s>bodhipakṣyadharma</s>)? Here, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, relying on the four analytical knowledges, truly knows the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening through knowledge encompassed by skillful means. Yet he does not directly realize them. He—

body.text:
dvividhenāpi yānanayena tān yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti śrāvakayānanayena ca mahāyānanayena ca / tatra śrāvakayānanayena yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti / tadyathā śrāvakabhūmau sarvaṃ yathā nirdiṣṭaṃ veditavyam / kathañca bodhisattvo mahāyānanayena
saptatriṃśadbodhipakṣyān dharmān yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti / iha bodhisattvaḥ kāye kāyānudarśī viharan naiva kāyaṃ kāyabhāvato vikalpayati / nāpi sarveṇa sarvamabhāvataḥ / tañca kāyanirabhilāpyasvabhāvadharmatāṃ yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti / iyamasya paramārthikī kāye kāyānupaśyanā smṛtyupasthānam / saṃvṛtinayena punarbodhisattvasyāpramāṇavyavasthāna-nayajñānānugataṃ kāye kāyānupaśyanā smṛtyupasthānaṃ veditavyam / yathā kāye kāyānupaśyanā smṛtyupasthānaṃ evamavaśiṣṭāni smṛtyupasthānāni aviśiṣṭāśca bodhipakṣyā dharmā veditavyāḥ / sa naiva kāyādīndharmān duḥkhato vā vikalpayati samudayato vā / nāpi tatkṛtaṃ prahāṇaṃ nirodhataḥ kalpayati / nāpi tatprāptihetuṃ mārgataḥ kalpayati / nirabhilāpyasvabhāvadharmatayā ca duḥkhadharmatāṃ samudayadharmatāṃ nirodhadharmatāṃ mārgadharmatāṃ yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti / iyamasya pāramārthikī bodhipakṣyabhāvanā-sanniśrayeṇa satyabhāvanā bhavati / saṃvṛttyā punarapramāṇavyavasthāna-nayajñānānugatā bodhisattvasya satyālambanabhāvanā dṛṣṭavyā /
body.translated_text: truly knows them through both vehicle-approaches: the approach of the <s>Śrāvaka</s>-vehicle and the approach of the <s>Mahāyāna</s>. Therein, he truly knows through the approach of the <s>Śrāvaka</s>-vehicle as taught in the <s>Śrāvakabhūmi</s>—all should be understood as described there. And how does the <s>Bodhisattva</s> truly know the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening through the approach of the <s>Mahāyāna</s>? Here, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, abiding in the contemplation of the body in the body, does not conceptualize the body as having bodily nature, nor does he [conceptualize it] as completely non-existent. He truly knows the <s>dharmatā</s> (nature of reality) of the body as inexpressible in its own-nature. This is his ultimate (<s>paramārthika</s>) foundation of mindfulness (<s>smṛtyupasthāna</s>) of contemplation of the body in the body. By the conventional approach, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body in the body is to be understood as accompanied by the knowledge of the method of infinite establishment. Just as the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body, so too the remaining foundations of mindfulness and the remaining factors conducive to awakening are to be understood. He does not conceptualize <s>dharmas</s> such as the body and so forth as suffering or as origin; nor does he conceptualize the abandonment accomplished thereby as cessation; nor does he conceptualize the cause of that attainment as the path. Yet through the <s>dharmatā</s> of inexpressible own-nature, he truly knows the <s>dharmatā</s> of suffering, the <s>dharmatā</s> of origin, the <s>dharmatā</s> of cessation, and the <s>dharmatā</s> of the path. This is his ultimate cultivation of the truths in reliance on the cultivation of factors conducive to awakening. By the conventional [approach], the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s cultivation with the truths as object is to be seen as accompanied by the knowledge of the method of infinite establishment.

body.text: tatra yā bodhisattvasyaiṣā dharmāṇāmevamavikalpanā so 'sya śamatho draṣṭavyaḥ / yacca tadyathābhūtajñānaṃ pāramārthikaṃ yacca tadapramāṇa-vyavasthānanayajñānaṃ dharmeṣu iyamasya vipaśyanā draṣṭavyā /
body.translated_text: Therein, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s non-conceptualization of <s>dharmas</s> in this way is to be seen as his <s>śamatha</s> (calm). And that ultimate knowledge as it truly is, and that knowledge of the method of infinite establishment regarding <s>dharmas</s>—this is to be seen as his <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight).

body.text: tatra bodhisattvasya samāsataścaturākāraḥ śamatho veditavyaḥ / pāramārthikasāṅketika-jñānapūrvaṅgamaḥ pāramārthikasāṃketika-jñānaphalaṃ sarvaprapañcasaṃjñāsu anābhogavāhanaḥ tasmiṃśca nirabhilāpye vastumātrai nirnimittatayā ca nirvikalpacittāśāntyā sarvadharmasamataikarasagāmī / ebhiścaturbhirākāraibodhisattvānāṃ śamathamārgaḥ pravartate yāvadanuttara-samyaksaṃbodhijñānadarśana-pariniṣpattaye samudāgamāya /
body.translated_text: Therein, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s <s>śamatha</s>, in brief, is to be known as fourfold: preceded by ultimate and conventional knowledge; being the fruit of ultimate and conventional knowledge; effortlessly flowing in all perceptions of conceptual proliferation; and, regarding that inexpressible mere entity, through signlessness and through the peace of the non-conceptual mind, proceeding as the single taste of the equality of all <s>dharmas</s>. Through these four aspects, the path of <s>śamatha</s> of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> operates, up to the completion and attainment of the knowledge-vision of unsurpassed perfect awakening.

body.text: tatra bodhisattvānāṃ samāsataścaturākāraiva vipaśyanā veditavyā / etaccaturākāra-śamathapūrvaṅgamā sarvadharmeṣu samāropāsadgrāhāntavivarjitā apavādāsadgrāhāntavivarjitā apramāṇadharmaprabhedavyavasthāna-nayānugatā ca vipaśyanā / ebhiścaturbhirākārai rbodhisattvānāṃ vipaśyanāmārgaḥ pravartate yāvadanuttara-samyaksaṃbodhijñānidarśana-[pari]niṣpattaye
body.translated_text: Therein, the <s>vipaśyanā</s> of <s>Bodhisattvas</s>, in brief, is to be known as likewise fourfold: preceded by this fourfold <s>śamatha</s>; free from the extreme of the wrong grasping of superimposition regarding all <s>dharmas</s>; free from the extreme of the wrong grasping of denial; and accompanied by the method of establishing infinite classifications of <s>dharmas</s>. Through these four aspects, the path of <s>vipaśyanā</s> of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> operates, up to the completion—

body.text: samudāgamāya / itīyaṃ bodhisattvānāṃ śamathavipaśyanā samāsanirdeśataḥ /
body.translated_text: and attainment of the knowledge-vision of unsurpassed perfect awakening. This is the summary teaching of the <s>Bodhisattvas</s>' <s>śamatha</s> and <s>vipaśyanā</s>.

body.text: tatra katamadbodhisattvānāmupāyakauśalyam / tatsamāsato dvādaśākāram / adhyātma-buddhadharmasamudāgamamārabhya [ṣaḍvidham /] bahirdhā-sattvaparipākamārabhya ṣaḍvidhameva /
body.translated_text: What therein is the <s>Bodhisattvas</s>' skill in means (<s>upāyakauśalya</s>)? In brief, it is twelvefold: sixfold with respect to the internal attainment of <s>Buddha</s>-qualities, and sixfold with respect to the external ripening of beings.

body.text: adhyātma-buddhadharmasamudāgamamārabhya ṣaḍvidhamupāyakauśalyaṃ katamat / yā bodhisattvasya sarvasattveṣu karuṇāsahagatā apekṣā yacca sarvasaṃskāreṣu yathābhūtasarvaparijñānaṃ yā cānuttarasamyaksaṃbodhijñāne spṛhā / yacca sattvāpekṣāṃ niśritya saṃsārāparityāgaḥ yā ca saṃskāreṣu yathābhūtaparijñānaṃ niśrityāsaṃkliṣṭacittasya saṃsārasaṃsṛtī / yā ca buddhajñāne spṛhā niśrityottaptavīryatā / idamadhyātmabuddhadharmaṃsamudāgamamārabhya ṣaḍivadhamupāyakauśalyaṃ veditavyam /
body.translated_text: What is the sixfold skill in means with respect to the internal attainment of <s>Buddha</s>-qualities? The <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s concern accompanied by compassion toward all beings; the true complete knowledge of all conditioned formations as they really are; the aspiration for the knowledge of unsurpassed perfect awakening; the non-abandonment of <s>saṃsāra</s> relying on concern for beings; the transmigration in <s>saṃsāra</s> with an undefiled mind relying on the true complete knowledge of conditioned formations; and the zealous energy relying on the aspiration for <s>Buddha</s>-knowledge. This is to be known as the sixfold skill in means with respect to the internal attainment of <s>Buddha</s>-qualities.

body.text: tatra katamadbahirdhā-sattvaparipākamārabhya ṣaḍvidhamupāyakauśalyam / yenopāyakauśalyena bodhisattvaḥ parāttāni kuśalamūlāni apramāṇaphalatāyāmupanayati / tathālpakṛcchreṇa vipulānyapramāṇāni kuśalamūlāni samāvartayatyupasaṃharati / tathā buddhaśāsanapratihatānāṃ sattvānāṃ pratighātamapanayati / madhyasthānavatārayati / avatīrṇān paripācayati / paripakvān vimocayati /
body.translated_text: What therein is the sixfold skill in means with respect to the external ripening of beings? The skill in means by which the <s>Bodhisattva</s> leads the small wholesome roots of others to immeasurable fruition; likewise, with little effort gathers and provides abundant, immeasurable wholesome roots; likewise, removes the obstruction of beings who are opposed to the <s>Buddha</s>'s teaching; brings in those who are neutral; ripens those who have entered; and liberates those who are ripened.

body.text: kathañca bodhisattvaḥ sattvānāṃ parīttāni kuśalamūlāni apramāṇaphalatāyāmupanayati / iha bodhisattvo yat kiṃcit sattvaṃ pratyavaramapi vastvantataḥ saktuprasṛtaṃ pratyavara eva kṣetre pradāpayati antatastiryagyonigate 'pi parīttaṃ tacca prāṇibhūte dāpayitvā cānuttarāyāṃ samyaksaṃmbodhau pariṇāmayati / evaṃ tatkuśalamūlaṃ vastuto 'pi kṣetrato 'pi parīttaṃ tacca pariṇāmanā-vaśenāpramāṇaphalatayāmupanītaṃ bhavati
body.translated_text: How does the <s>Bodhisattva</s> lead the small wholesome roots of beings to immeasurable fruition? Here, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> causes any being to give even a small, inferior object—even a handful of barley-flour—to even an inferior field, even to an animal, to even a small, living creature; and having caused the gift, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed perfect awakening. Thus, that wholesome root, though small in terms of both the object and the field, through the power of dedication, is led to immeasurable fruition.

body.text: kathaṃ ca bodhisattvaḥ sattvānāmalpakṛcchreṇa vipulānyapramāṇāni kuśalamūlāni saṃjanayati / iha bodhisattvo mithyā-māsopavāsānaśanādyadhimuktānāṃ sattvānāmāryāṣṭāṅgamupavāsaṃ vyapadiśati / tasmādvicchandayati kṛcchrādaniṣṭaphalādupavāsāt / tasminnakṛcchrasamādāne mahāphale copavāse samādāpayati / tathā ātmaklamathayogamanuyuktānāṃ mokṣakāmānāṃ mithyāprayuktānāṃ [sattvānāṃ]
body.translated_text: How does the <s>Bodhisattva</s> generate abundant, immeasurable wholesome roots for beings with little effort? Here, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> prescribes the noble eightfold observance (<s>upavāsa</s>) to beings inclined toward wrong monthly fasts, starvation, and such; he dissuades them from that difficult fast of undesirable fruit and causes them to undertake that easy observance of great fruit. Likewise, to those who pursue self-mortification, who desire liberation but are wrongly engaged—

body.text: madhyamāṃ pratipadamantadvayavigatāṃ vyapadiśati tasyāṃ cāvatārayati / tathā svargakāmānāṃ [sattvānāṃ] mithyāprayuktānāmagnipraveśātaṭaprapātā 'naśanasthānādibhiḥ samyagdhyānaṃ dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihārāya cāyatyāṃ akṛchreṇa sahaiva sukhena saha saumanasyena svargopapattaye vyapadiśati / punarvaidikamantroddeśasvādhyāyaśuddhiniṣṭhāgamanādhimuktān buddhavacanoddeśasvādhyāyakriyāyāmarthacintāyāñca samādāpayati / punargambhīrāṃstathāgatabhāṣitān śūnyatāpratisaṃyuktāndharmān tathā tathā uttānīkaroti saṃprakāśayati yathā pare śrutvā tīvrañca saṃvegamutpādayanti tīvraṃ ca prasādam / tadekakṣaṇikamapi saṃvegaprasādasahagataṃ cittaṃ vipula[kuśamūla]saṃgrahe saṃkhyāṃ gacchati prāgeva prābandhikam / punarbodhisattvo yāni kānicinmālyāni gandhajātāni ca loke vividhāni pravarāṇi praṇītāni taiḥ prasādasahagatenādhyāśayena buddhadharmasaṃgha[tri]ratnapūjāmadhimucyate parāṃścādhimocayati daśasu dikṣu / punaḥ sarvā diśastenaiva prasādasahagatenādhyāśayena spharitvā sarvāṃ triratnapūjāmabhyanumodate parāṃścābhyanumodayati / punarbuddhānusmṛtiṃ satatasamitaṃ bhāvayati pareṣāñca samādāpayati dharmānusmṛtiṃ saṃghānusmṛtiṃ yāvaddevatānusmṛtim / punarmanojalpaistriratna-namaskriyayā abandhyaṃ kālaṃ karoti kārayati ca / punaḥ sarvasattvānāṃ sarvapuṇyamanumodate anumodayati ca / punaḥ sarvasattvānāṃ vipulakaruṇānupraviṣṭenādhyāśayena sarvaduḥkhamātmani saṃpratīcchati / tatraiva paraṃ samādāpayati / punaratītapratyutpannāni sarva-skhalitāni sarvavyatikramāṃśca kalyāṇena śikṣākāmānugatena cetasā sarvadikṣu buddhānāṃ bhagavatāmantike pratideśayati / tatraiva ca parān samādāpayati / tasyaivamabhīkṣṇaṃ skhalitaṃ pratideśayataḥ sarvakarmāvaraṇebhyo vimokṣo bhavatyalpakṛcchreṇa / punaḥ prabhūtairvicitraiśca nirmāṇaiḥ sarvadikṣu buddhadharmasaṃghādhiṣṭhānaṃ sattvādhiṣṭhānañcāprameyaṃ bodhisattvaḥ ṛddhimāṃścetovaśiprāptaḥ puṇyaparigrahaṃ karoti / punarbodhisattvaḥ maitrīṃ karuṇāṃ muditāmupekṣāṃ bhāvayati / tatraiva ca paraṃ samādāpayati / evaṃ hi bodhisattvo 'lpakṛcchreṇa vipulānyaprameyaphalāni kuśalamūlānyabhinirharati samudānayati /
body.translated_text: he prescribes the middle path free from the two extremes and brings them into it. Likewise, to those who desire heaven but are wrongly engaged, through fire-entering, cliff-jumping, starvation, and such, he prescribes correct meditation for pleasant abiding in this present life and for rebirth in heaven in the future, without hardship, together with ease and mental pleasure. Furthermore, he causes those inclined toward the recitation, study, and purification-attainment of Vedic mantras to undertake the recitation and study of the word of the <s>Buddha</s> and the contemplation of its meaning. Furthermore, he elucidates and illuminates the profound <s>dharmas</s> spoken by the <s>Tathāgata</s>, connected with emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>), in such a way that others, having heard, generate both intense spiritual urgency and intense faith. Even a single moment of mind accompanied by urgency and faith counts among the gathering of vast wholesome roots, how much more so when continuous. Furthermore, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, with whatever flowers and fragrances that are various, excellent, and noble in the world, with the superior intention accompanied by faith, imagines the worship of the Three Jewels—the <s>Buddha</s>, <s>Dharma</s>, and <s>Saṃgha</s>—in the ten directions and causes others to do likewise. Furthermore, pervading all directions with that very superior intention accompanied by faith, he rejoices in (<s>anumodana</s>) all worship of the Three Jewels and causes others to rejoice. Furthermore, he constantly cultivates the recollection of the <s>Buddha</s> and causes others to undertake it—the recollection of the <s>Dharma</s>, the <s>Saṃgha</s>, up to the recollection of the gods. Furthermore, through mental salutations to the Three Jewels, he makes time fruitful and causes others to do so. Furthermore, he rejoices in all the merit of all beings and causes others to rejoice. Furthermore, with the superior intention pervaded by vast compassion toward all beings, he takes upon himself all their suffering, and causes others to do likewise. Furthermore, with a wholesome mind accompanied by the desire for training, he confesses all past and present stumbles and transgressions in the presence of the <s>Buddhas</s>, the <s>Bhagavāns</s>, in all directions; and causes others to do likewise. By thus frequently confessing stumbles, liberation from all <s>karma</s>-obscurations occurs with little effort. Furthermore, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> who possesses supernatural power and has attained mental mastery, with abundant and various magical creations, gathers an immeasurable collection of merit through the support of the <s>Buddha</s>, <s>Dharma</s>, <s>Saṃgha</s>, and the support of beings in all directions. Furthermore, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> cultivates loving-kindness (<s>maitrī</s>), compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>), sympathetic joy (<s>muditā</s>), and equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>), and causes others to undertake the same. Thus the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, with little effort, brings forth and gathers vast, immeasurably fruitful wholesome roots.

body.text: kathañca bodhisattvaḥ pratihatānāñca sattvānāṃ pratighātamapanayati / madhyasthāṃścāvatārayati / avatīrṇāṃśca paripācayati / parikvāṃśca vimocayati /
body.translated_text: How does the <s>Bodhisattva</s> remove the obstruction of beings who are opposed [to the teaching]? Bring in those who are neutral? Ripen those who have entered? And liberate those who are ripened?

body.text: atrāpi bodhisattvasya caturvidhasyāpyasya sattvārthasyābhiniṣpattaye samāsataḥ ṣaḍvidha evopāyo veditavyaḥ / ānulomiko vibandhasthāyī visabhāgāśayaḥ avaṣṭambhajaḥ kṛtaprakṛtikaḥ viśuddhaśca ṣaṣṭha upāyaḥ /
body.translated_text: Here too, for the accomplishment of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s fourfold welfare of beings, the skillful means should be understood as sixfold in brief: the conforming means (<s>ānulomika</s>), the obstacle-based means (<s>vibandhasthāyī</s>), the contrary-intention means (<s>visabhāgāśaya</s>), the compulsion-born means (<s>avaṣṭambhaja</s>), the action-and-reaction means (<s>kṛtaprakṛtika</s>), and the pure means (<s>viśuddha</s>) as the sixth.

body.text: tatrāyaṃ bodhisattvasyānulomika upāyaḥ / iha bodhisattvaḥ pūrvameva tāvad yeṣāṃ sattvānāṃ dharmaṃ deśayitukāmo bhavati teṣāṃ ślakṣṇairmadhuraiḥ kāyavāksamudācārairupapradānānuvṛttisamudācāraiścātmagataṃ teṣāṃ pratighātamapanayati / pratighātamapanīya premagaurava janayati / premagauravaṃ janayitvā dharme 'rthitvaṃ janayati / tata eṣāṃ paścāddharmaṃ deśayati / tañca punardharmaṃ yathārhaṃ supraveśaṃ gamakaṃ kālenānupūrvamaviparītamarthopasaṃhitañca deśayati / vimardasahiṣṇuśca bhavati / sattvavinaye paramayā ca kartukāmatayā anukampācittena samanvāgato bhavati / sa ṛddhyā cittādeśanayā yuktarūpayā dharmadeśanayā paraṃ vā 'dhyeṣya vicitrairvā prabhūtaiśca nirmitaiḥ sattvānvinayati / saṃkṣiptānāñcārthopasaṃhitānāṃ śāstrāṇāṃ pravistaraṇatayā ativistṛtānāṃ cābhisaṃkṣepaṇatayā tathā uddeśadānena anusmaraṇaparipṛcchādānena dhṛtānāñcodgṛhītānāñca dharmāṇāṃ samyagarthavivaraṇatayā sarvālambanasamādhyavatāramukheṣucānulomikyā avavādānusāsanyā sattvānanugṛhṇāti sattvānāmarthamācarati / ye ca sattvā gambhīrāṇāṃ tathāgatabhāṣitānāṃ śūnyatāpratisaṃyuktānāṃ sūtrāntānāmābhiprāyikaṃ tathāgatānāmarthamavijñāya ye te sūtrāntāḥ niḥsvabhāvatāṃ dharmāṇāmabhivadanti nirvastukatāmanutpannāniruddhatāmā kāśasamatāṃ māyāsvapnopamatāṃ dharmāṇāmabhivadanti teṣāṃ yathāvadarthamavijñāyotrastamānasāḥ tān sūtrāntān sarveṇa sarvaṃ pratikṣipanti naite tathāgatabhāṣitā iti / teṣāmapi sattvānāṃ sa bodhisattvaḥ ānulomikenopāyakauśalyena teṣāṃ sūtrāntānāṃ tathāgatābhiprāyikamarthaṃ yathāvadanulomayati /
body.translated_text: There, this is the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s conforming means (<s>ānulomika upāya</s>). Here, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, first of all, with gentle and sweet conduct of body and speech, and with conduct of giving and accommodation, removes the inner resistance of those beings to whom he wishes to teach the <s>Dharma</s>. Having removed their resistance, he generates love and reverence [in them]. Having generated love and reverence, he generates desire for the <s>Dharma</s> [in them]. Then afterward he teaches them the <s>Dharma</s>. And he teaches that <s>Dharma</s> as appropriate — easy to enter, penetrating, timely, gradual, undistorted, and connected with meaning. And he is patient with criticism. He is endowed with the supreme desire to act and with a mind of compassion for the discipline of beings. He disciplines beings through supernatural power (<s>ṛddhi</s>), through the reading of minds (<s>cittādeśanā</s>), through appropriate <s>Dharma</s>-teaching, or by inviting others [to teach], or through various and abundant magical creations. By expanding upon brief treatises connected with meaning, by condensing those that are overly extensive, by giving summaries (<s>uddeśa</s>), by providing occasions for recollection and questioning, by correctly explaining the meaning of <s>dharmas</s> that have been retained and mastered, and by conforming instruction and admonition regarding all the entry-points of <s>samādhi</s> on all objects — he benefits beings and acts for their welfare. And those beings who, not understanding the intended meaning of the <s>Tathāgatas</s>' profound discourses connected with emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>) — those <s>sūtras</s> that declare the lack of intrinsic nature (<s>niḥsvabhāvatā</s>) of <s>dharmas</s>, their lack of substantial reality, their unborn and unceased nature, their equality with space, and their likeness to illusion and dreams — who, not understanding their true meaning, become frightened and alarmed, and reject those <s>sūtras</s> entirely, [saying:] 'These are not spoken by the <s>Tathāgata</s>' — for those beings too, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, through conforming skill in means, properly elucidates the intended meaning of the <s>Tathāgatas</s> in those <s>sūtras</s>.

body.text: tāṃśca sattvān grāhayati / evañca punaranulomayati / yathā neme dharmāḥ sarveṇa sarvaṃ na saṃvidyante api tvabhilāpātmakaḥ svabhāva eṣāṃ nāsti teneme niḥsvabhāvā ityucyante / yadyapyetavabhilāpyavastu vidyate yadāśrityābhilāpāḥ pravartante tadapi yairabhilāpairyat svabhāvamabhilapyate tadapi na tatsvabhāva paramārthataḥ / tasmānnirvastukā ityucyante evañca sati te 'bhilāpyāḥ svabhāvā dharmāṇāmādita eva sarveṇa
body.translated_text: And he makes those beings understand. And he elucidates in this manner: 'It is not that these <s>dharmas</s> do not exist at all in every respect. Rather, their intrinsic nature as verbal designation (<s>abhilāpa</s>) does not exist — therefore they are called lacking intrinsic nature (<s>niḥsvabhāva</s>). Although the object that is designated exists — that upon which designations operate — even that, the intrinsic nature by which it is designated through those designations, that too is not ultimately its intrinsic nature. Therefore they are called lacking substantial reality (<s>nirvastukatā</s>). And this being so, those designated intrinsic natures of <s>dharmas</s> do not exist at all from the very beginning.

body.text: sarvaṃ na saṃvidyante / te kimutpatsyante vā nirotsyante vā tasmādanutpannā aniruddhā ityucyante / tadyathā cākāśe vicitrāṇi prabhūtāni rūpāṇi rūpakarmāṇi copalabhyante / sarveṣāñca teṣāṃ rūpāṇāṃ rūpakarmaṇāṃ cāvakāśaṃ dadāti / tadākāśaṃ gamanāgamanasthānotpatananipatanākuñcanaprasāraṇādīnām / yadā ca punastad rūpaṃ tāni ca rūpakarmāṇyapanītāni bhavanti tadā rūpābhāvamātrātmakameva pariśuddhamākāśaṃ khyāti / evaṃ tasminnākāśasthānīye nirabhilāpye vastuni vividhābhilāpakṛtāḥ saṃjñā vikalpāḥ prapañcasaṃjñānugatāḥ rūpakarmasthānīyāḥ pravartante / sarveṣāñca teṣāmabhilāpakṛtānāṃ saṃjñāvikalpānāṃ prapañcasaṃjñānugatānāṃ citrarūpakarmasthānīyānāṃ tannirabhilāpyaṃ vastvākāśa sthānīyamavakāśaṃ dadāti / yadā ca punarbodhisattvairjñānenāryeṇa te 'bhilāpasamutthitā mithyāsaṃjñāvikalpāḥ prapañcasaṃjñānugatāḥ sarveṇa sarvamapanītā bhavanti tadā teṣāṃ bodhisattvānāṃ paramāryāṇāṃ tenāryajñānena tannirabhilāpyaṃ vastu sarvābhilāpyasvabhāvābhāvamātramākāśopamaṃ pariśuddhaṃ khyāti / na ca tasmāt paramanyaṃ svabhāvamasya mṛgayante / tasmāddharmā ākāśa samā ityucyante / tadyathā māyā na ca yathā khyāti tathāsti / na ca punaḥ sarveṇaiva sarvaṃ nāsti tanmāyākṛtam / evaṃ na caite dharmā yathaivābhilāpasaṃstavavaśena khyānti bālānāṃ tathaiva saṃvidyante / na ca punaḥ sarveṇa sarvaṃ na saṃvidyante pāramārthika-nirabhilāpyātmanā / te cānena nayapraveśena na santo nāsanta ityadvayā māyāvat / tasmānmāyopamā ityucyante / evaṃ hi bodhisattvaḥ sarvasmāddharmadhātorna kiñcidutkṣipati na ca kiñcit pratikṣipati nonī-karoti nādhikaṃ karoti na vināśayati / bhūtañca bhūtataḥ prajānāti / tathaiva ca saṃprakāśayati / ayaṃ bodhisattvasyānulomika upāyo veditavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: How then could they arise or cease? Therefore they are called unborn and unceased (<s>anutpanna-aniruddha</s>). Just as in space, various and abundant forms and activities of forms are perceived, and that space provides room for all those forms and their activities — for going and coming, standing and rising, falling, contracting, extending, and so forth — yet when those forms and those activities of forms are removed, space appears as pure, consisting merely in the absence of form; so too, in that inexpressible (<s>nirabhilāpya</s>) reality which is like space, various conceptualizations and proliferating notions (<s>prapañcasaṃjñā</s>) created by verbal designation, which are like the activities of forms, operate. And that inexpressible reality, like space, provides room for all those conceptualizations and proliferating notions created by verbal designation, which are like the various activities of forms. But when those false conceptualizations and proliferating notions arising from verbal designation are entirely removed by the noble knowledge of <s>Bodhisattvas</s>, then for those supremely noble <s>Bodhisattvas</s>, through that noble knowledge, that inexpressible reality appears as pure — consisting merely in the absence of all intrinsic natures that are objects of designation — like space.
